Alliance aims to accelerate the creation of scientifically relevant quantum computers by 2028 as part of the Department of Energy’s Quantum Genesis Mission. Leading quantum companies see error correction as a key step toward that goal.

IBM, AMD, and the U.S. Department of Energy (DoE)-funded Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) announced on Nov. 5 a new quantum/AI platform aimed at improving quantum error correction, an emerging focus for the industry.

Researchers are making advances in error correction, including early demonstrations that protect quantum information from noise. IBM claims quantum advantage using techniques with guaranteed correctness, showing that quantum computers integrated with classical computers can solve relevant problems better than classical systems alone. The partners aim to amp up progress by bringing more classical computing into the mix.

The project at the Oak Ridge laboratory co-locates IBM’s quantum computers, including the company’s most powerful quantum processor, the 120-qubit IBM Quantum Nighthawk, with ORNL’s Umbra HPC system, running AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs. AMD provides the classical computing foundation for research into error correction, decoding optimization, and software orchestration.

A quantum error is caused by disruptions to the delicate quantum state of a qubit, which operates near absolute zero. Qubits typically need temperatures between 10 and 20 millikelvin (–273.15°C or –459.67°F).

The co-designed platform under development at Oak Ridge in the U.S. state of Tennessee will let researchers evaluate how to knit together classical and quantum computing to advance quantum error correction. The effort supports the DOE’s Quantum Genesis Mission, which targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. IBM said it has demonstrated experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations. For the partners to reach the DoE target, they will need to achieve a roughly 230-fold increase in hard-operation count.

“Today, the question is how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle meaningful problems,” Jay Gambetta, IBM Research director, said in a press statement. “This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software, and workflows that will scale.”

Hard operations

In quantum computing, resource theory divides operations into easy (Clifford) and hard (non-Clifford) sets.

Non-Clifford operations are particularly resource-intensive in fault-tolerant quantum computing because they cannot generally be implemented as cheaply as Clifford operations and require additional error-correction resources, Seetharami Seelam, chief architect of Classical System Co-Design for Quantum-Centric Supercomputing at IBM, told EE Times.

All error-correcting codes admit instructions that are cheap to implement and others that are expensive. So, what is “hard” is a result of the choice of code on any given platform, Seelam noted.

Next era

The next era of computing will combine quantum computing with decades of innovation across the classical hardware and software ecosystem, AMD EVP Mark Papermaster said.

“We are advancing a holistic approach that integrates quantum processors, HPC, and AI,” Papermaster noted. “This co-design platform is an important step toward building the scalable, efficient computing infrastructure needed to make fault-tolerant quantum computing a reality.”

Solving quantum error-correction challenges is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, and that’s a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, according to Travis Humble, director of the Quantum Science Center at ORNL.

Oak Ridge and AMD are partners in what was possibly the world’s first “exascale” computer.

Europe has led the concept of hybrid classical/quantum computing, as Czechia, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg are working to deploy on-site quantum computers that are integrated with classical supercomputing under the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking, the Center for Strategic & International Studies, a Washington, DC think tank, noted in a March 2026 report.

IBM had a less geopolitical view.

“IBM has been leading the way in developing quantum-centric supercomputing for several years, including a reference architecture for integrating quantum processors with CPUs and GPUs into HPC environments that has been used in deployments in both Europe and Japan,” Seelam said. “The ORNL collaboration represents an important next step in applying that approach in the U.S., bringing IBM quantum computers together with ORNL’s high-performance computing infrastructure and AMD CPUs and GPUs.”

Focus on error correction

Leading quantum computing companies see error correction as a critical step toward the first quantum applications that are scientifically and commercially relevant.

Through 2029, Quantinuum expects its Nexus quantum system to automate and simplify error correction, resource management, orchestration, and deployment, enabling developers to build and integrate increasingly capable applications at the logical level.

$2 billion

IBM and Quantinuum are among nine U.S. companies that got $2 billion from the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump to secure the nation’s quantum leadership.

Quantinuum’s Nexus system supports more than 200 organizations, a 45% increase this year, while total job submissions increased tenfold in the 12 months through August 2026 compared with the preceding 12-month period, the company said today in a press release.

“Quantum computers are on the brink of achieving fault tolerance at scale,” José Ignacio Latorre, director of Singapore’s Centre for Quantum Technologies, said in the press release. “It’s exciting: we are entering terra incognita for what we can compute. The new challenge is putting our high-level quantum algorithms into the right form to successfully run on error-corrected hardware. Developer platforms like Nexus help us bridge that gap between quantum algorithm design and deployment.”

IBM said Nighthawk’s high maximum circuit throughput and real-time pulse control enable researchers to test error-correction techniques. Researchers will compare what each technique requires in qubits, time, samples, and classical resources to learn where GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help the most.

IBM said researchers can use the company’s quantum hardware to measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing of the signals that protect qubits from noise, see exactly what the hardware ran, and work directly with raw measurement signals.

Solid partners

The new co-design platform for quantum error correction builds on IBM’s existing collaborations with ORNL and AMD.

Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL demonstrated how workloads running on quantum computers and ORNL’s Frontier supercomputer can simulate magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of promising materials for the production of fusion fuel.

IBM has been using AMD GPUs to accelerate the classical diagonalization step in sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), a key quantum-centric supercomputing workflow. Last year, the two companies demonstrated an algorithm that efficiently decodes quantum errors on AMD chips. IBM said the partners’ effort with error correction and HPC workflows may support IBM’s path to its Quantum Starling system, the company’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer

data.title: Europe’s Chip Industry: Perfect Storm or Perfect Timing?
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

On the afternoon of Oct. 28, 1991, a low-pressure system began forming east of Nova Scotia, Canada, as Hurricane Grace gathered strength just west of Bermuda. Over New England, a cool, dry air mass settled in, and a high-pressure system built over the Great Lakes. As American journalist and author Sebastian Junger recounts in “The Perfect Storm,” none of these were exceptional on their own. Yet their convergence produced one of the fiercest storms on record.

SEMICON Europa 2026, co-located with electronica 2026 in Munich from Nov. 10 to 13, takes the meteorological event as its central metaphor: “Europe’s Next Era: Navigating the Perfect Storm.” The theme reflects the semiconductor industry’s mounting geopolitical, technological, and competitive pressures.

The warning is not new. At the CxO Summit during SEMICON Europa 2025, Laith Altimime, president of SEMI Europe, described the continent as caught “in a perfect storm.” He said, “As we face a combination of internal challenges and intensifying external competition, collaboration is not optional; it is mission-critical.”

Overdependence and a structural competitiveness gap form the low-pressure system, or Nor’easter. According to a European Commission analysis published in June 2026, total fab production costs in EU fabs are 40% to 50% higher than in Taiwan, South Korea, and China. Europe’s reliance on overseas suppliers is equally stark. In 2024, the EU consumed €55 billion worth of semiconductors and imported €43.6 billion from outside the bloc. Its vulnerability is greatest in leading-edge chips for AI and high-performance computing.

Geopolitical turbulence is the high-pressure system. The European Commission’s 2026 Annual Single Market and Competitiveness Report describes how major powers use tariffs, export controls, and supply chain dependencies as instruments of economic leverage. Russia’s war against Ukraine, military tensions in the Taiwan Strait, conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, U.S. technology restrictions, and China’s expanding manufacturing capacity expose Europe’s semiconductor ecosystem to external risks. Europe must navigate between U.S. investment, China’s industrial ambitions, and its own pursuit of technological sovereignty.

The fallout from the first Chips Act represents the lingering effects of Hurricane Grace. In 2025, the European Court of Auditors concluded that “the strategy is very unlikely to be sufficient to achieve by 2030 the very ambitious Digital Decade target of a 20% EU share in the global market value chain by revenue.” The EU’s share is now projected to reach just 11.7% by 2030.

Whether the metaphor holds is the question the conference sets out to test: Is Europe the Andrea Gail, or can it read the forecast and chart a different course?

The proposed Chips Act 2.0, published in June 2026 and targeted for adoption in the second quarter of 2027, does not abandon advanced manufacturing but recalibrates the strategy around a wider set of industrial and policy priorities.

The European Commission’s proposal broadens the focus beyond the race for advanced fabs to the entire semiconductor value chain, from chip design and manufacturing equipment to materials and advanced packaging. It also aims to bridge Europe’s lab-to-fab gap by scaling up pilot lines and bringing research closer to commercial production. Rather than pursuing market share alone, the strategy seeks to secure critical capabilities in both leading-edge and mature-node chips and connect chipmakers more closely with customers in automotive, industrial systems, and data centers. Better access to patient capital could help startups scale up and “create the conditions required for high-potential technology businesses to emerge.”

“Europe’s semiconductor competitiveness depends on the strength of the entire ecosystem, from design and materials to equipment, manufacturing, and advanced packaging,” Altimime said. “The Chips Act 2.0 provides an important opportunity to build on Europe’s existing strengths. Our recommendations aim to ensure that the new framework delivers the speed, investment, and policy certainty needed to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness and resilience.”

Europe does not need to do everything. It needs to be pragmatic about where it can compete, clear-eyed about where demand is growing, and ready to build on its synergies and act together. Navigating the perfect storm will require a common course.

The EU’s motto offers a fitting conclusion: in varietate concordia—united in diversity.

As the semiconductor industry gathers in Munich for SEMICON Europa and electronica 2026, the November 2026 Edition of EE Times Magazine opens with a look at advances in semiconductor manufacturing and packaging. We examine Applied Materials’ $5 billion EPIC Center in Silicon Valley, ASM International’s work on 3D structures, and a Fraunhofer-IMS Nanofabrication partnership supporting advanced chipmaking. 

Our Special Report, Sowing the Seeds of Farm Autonomy, explores how sensing, embedded computing, connectivity, and AI give farmers greater control over agricultural operations. Farmers can now monitor and manage machinery, irrigation, pest and weed detection, fertilizer use, crop health, storage, and even global cereal production and trade in real time to support more informed decisions. Yet key questions persist: How safe are autonomous tractors, robots, and AI-guided machines? Can edge AI make agricultural data processing more efficient and sustainable? Could quantum sensing provide the detection sensitivity and processing power needed to overcome current limits? The report draws on interviews with industry players and researchers to assess the engineering requirements and remaining barriers, including machine safety, connectivity in rural areas, processing capacity, and equipment costs.

Finally, a report examines Canada’s efforts to connect its strengths in quantum computing, photonics, advanced materials, and ocean electronics. From quantum hardware and AI-guided materials discovery to electronics designed for remote and demanding environments, the report covers developments across the country and persistent obstacles, including capital, talent, infrastructure, and commercialization. The report also asks what it will take to move Canadian research out of the lab and into domestic production.

data.title: Nvidia, Municipal Leaders Frame AI as Critical Urban Infrastructure
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

BARCELONA, Spain — At the Smart City Expo World Congress, executives from Nvidia and municipal officials from Europe and the U.S. made the case for AI as an indispensable component of civic infrastructure.

With a keynote by Paolo Guglielmini, Nvidia’s VP for EMEA, and an executive panel moderated by Michael Lake, CEO of Leading Cities, the summit emphasized the need for local governments to establish centralized computing facilities—termed “AI factories”—to turn vast volumes of urban data into civic operational decisions, maintain sovereignty over sensitive municipal data, and retain technical talent rather than see it move to private technology centers.

Municipal data gap and architecture

In a keynote titled “From AI Factories to Intelligent Cities,” Guglielmini described what he called a structural bottleneck in modern municipal governance: the disparity between the raw data cities collect and the fraction they analyze to guide civic operations.

“Your organizations, your city’s municipalities, and regions have never had so much data available to you,” said Guglielmini, pointing to continuous streams from water utilities, air quality monitors, traffic sensors, mobile devices, GPS trackers, and satellite imagery. “But the gap between the data that’s available and the data that we use for decision-making has never been this great.”

To close that operational gap, Guglielmini proposed a five-layer architectural model for civic technology: energy, compute hardware, foundational infrastructure, software models, and end-user applications. He noted that while cities invest heavily in hardware, much of the economic value is created at the application level.

“Economic opportunity will happen where compute resides,” Guglielmini said. “Talent will stay where compute infrastructure is built. The lion’s share of startups created today are AI-native startups, and entrepreneurs and innovators will always follow where infrastructure is built.”

Addressing the technical friction within city halls, Guglielmini said legacy administrative systems often hinder modernization. “Very often, the organizations you are within have a lot of legacy,” Guglielmini said. “We have data that is nested. We have silos. We have applications built over tens of years. AI is perfect to build that layer on top that harnesses the power of data.”

From digital twins to language agents

To illustrate how localized computing can translate into municipal operations, Guglielmini detailed three distinct deployments across European regions.

In the Doubs department in eastern France, regional authorities built digital replicas of more than 500 public buildings, according to Guglielmini. Rather than relying solely on structural geometry, the digital mock-ups integrate real-time utility records, maintenance histories, and environmental metrics. “This is not about pure geometry,” Guglielmini said. “These are mock-ups that are enriched with data maintenance, data records, and utility records. Simulating cities and urban planning into the future has never become so affordable, so quick, and so valuable.”

In Palermo, Italy, municipal authorities established a center of excellence that uses a real-time AI model to process feeds from cameras and multiple types of sensors. The system combines urban monitoring with traffic management, emergency response dispatching, and municipal waste tracking. “Palermo went off and built a center of excellence that is incredibly capable of fusing sensor data from a multiplicity of facets and really shorten the time to emergency response,” Guglielmini explained.

In Barcelona, municipal technology developer 1 Million Bots deployed an agentic service platform built on “Laia,” a specialized language model developed at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. The model was trained specifically to handle regional administrative procedures in Spanish and regional languages, including Catalan, Galician, and Basque.

“Laia is a model that is highly specialized and highly sovereign for the Spanish language, and for all the [languages] that are important to address the largest possible population of your citizens,” Guglielmini said. He emphasized that local hosting keeps public data secure: “The city is in control of the applications, in control of the data, and in control of the permitting and permissions of who gets to see that data.”

Moving from pilot projects to reality

Following the keynote, Michael Lake, president and chief executive of Leading Cities, convened an executive panel titled “By the City, for the City: Making AI Work.” Lake organized the discussion around three core principles: Purpose, Power, and Proof.

“Technology doesn’t fail because it’s bad,” Lake said. “Technologies and communities fail because the system that it needs to survive is not ready for it.”

Charbel Aoun, director of smart cities and spaces for EMEA at Nvidia, criticized municipalities’ tendency to treat AI as a series of disconnected software pilot projects rather than integrating them into their operations—a pattern panel members characterized as “death by a thousand pilots.”

“Most of the pilots end up being a lessons-learned paper,” Aoun said. “What we need to prove is the value and the adoption.” 

Aoun argued that cities should treat computing capacity as foundational civic infrastructure, comparable to electrical grids or water lines. “AI is becoming critical infrastructure,” Aoun noted. “If we achieve that point, then we need to learn from the broadband mistake and from previous mistakes. Cities can own it, rent it, or partner, but they need an AI factory foundation.”

U.S. cities focus on productivity and public safety

Panel members from American cities described pragmatic approaches designed to establish public trust and streamline labor-intensive municipal tasks.

Mayor Keith A. James of West Palm Beach, Fla., said his administration chose public records processing as its first application. Municipal staff members handle extensive paperwork under strict legal timelines, making document retrieval a natural fit for automation.

“Cities tend to be very labor-intensive or paper-intensive,” James said. “You want to show the residents the AI working, and you want to begin with realistic applications. Our project involves public records requests. It helps our residents because we respond efficiently, and it takes some of the burden off our staff.”

In Tampa, Fla., Mayor Jane Castor said public safety departments have led municipal technology adoption because of immediate operational demands. Tampa recently deployed an automated drone response system linked directly to its real-time crime center, allowing aerial units to reach emergency scenes ahead of ground vehicles.

To prevent department silos, Tampa is also deploying “Iris,” a software platform that consolidates data from water quality, wastewater, solid waste, purchasing, and permitting into a single executive dashboard.

Castor emphasized that clear boundaries are vital to maintaining public confidence. “You have to share information with your community so that trust is there,” Castor said. “They shouldn’t feel like there’s a surveillance state in your community.”

European AI strategies in universities and communities

European municipal leaders highlighted frameworks that link technology deployment directly to academic institutions and geographic equity.

First Deputy Mayor Jakub Mazur of Wrocław, Poland, detailed how his administration replaced ad hoc software trials with a citywide strategy anchored by the Wrocław University of Science and Technology and its 25,000 students. The city deployed an AI-assisted enrollment system that handles 95% of school placements for local families, while encouraging technical graduates to remain in the regional economy.

Mazur stressed that decisions affecting citizens must remain accountable to elected officials, not automated systems.

“We need to own it because the city is responsible for data and the decision-making process,” Mazur stated. “We are democratically elected; we can be voted out. The algorithm cannot be voted out.”

For Rome, Italy, Deputy Mayor Valeria Baglio outlined a strategy focused on neighborhood-wide inclusion. Rather than concentrating digital investments in tourist-heavy central districts, Rome’s strategy extends digital public services across outer residential areas.

Rome’s initiative operates through “CTE Roma“, or Houses of Innovation, a municipal network linking city government, regional universities, startup incubators, and living labs. “We are working to bring digital services closer to residents across all districts, so that innovation isn’t just focused around central stations or downtown hubs,” Baglio said.

Building infrastructure for long-term value

To conclude his keynote, Guglielmini said that building municipal computing infrastructure doesn’t necessarily require a multi-gigawatt capital investment right away. He urged city officials to consider a modular rollout approach.

“Your AI journey can start from something very small—something portable and powerful,” Guglielmini said, noting that numerous European technology enterprises began operations using compact desktop supercomputing units. “Adding the right level of ambition is fundamental, but getting started with a use case that is really transformational for your communities and thinking about it in modular terms is fundamental to get going.”

Looking ahead, Guglielmini said he expects the next decade of urban technology to focus less on experimentation and more on deploying permanent, on-the-ground computing assets to support urban productivity and growth.

“Infrastructure build-out for the next 10 years is going to mean building intelligence that is at your fingertips to help you run your cities more effectively and economically,” Guglielmini said. “Focus on the use cases that are most transformational for where you are, bring together the right ecosystem, and look at the resources you have available to build compute capacity that serves your community.”

data.title: What Makes a Quantum Company Valuable?
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Ahead of the World Quantum Festival 2026 in Cannes, France, quantum investors weighed technical bottlenecks, commercial timing, and customer adoption, with healthcare offering a revealing test.

Nardo Manaloto, managing partner of Qubits Ventures, asked the founder of an unnamed startup for a commercial roadmap. The startup was building a photonic quantum computer and had said it would need a decade to deliver its ultimate product. Manaloto wanted to know what the company could sell along the way.

The startup proposed a sequence beginning with a photon detector, followed by a chip, before progressing toward the computer itself. For Manaloto, each intermediate product must solve a customer problem and have commercial value on its own while advancing the company’s long-term technology roadmap.

“The roadmap also extends to the business side,” he told EE Times.

That requirement captures a central challenge in quantum investment. Scientific progress can make a technology promising, but building a valuable company also calls for judgments about customers, financing, and timing.

Finding the bottleneck

Owen Lozman, managing partner of Copenhagen-based quantum investment fund 55 North, draws on his experience in semiconductor investing. He looks for startups that can solve an industry bottleneck by the time customers urgently need a solution.

“Generally in deep tech, we’re not looking for, ‘Does the invention work?’ but, ‘Does it solve a problem at the time at which it’s going to be needed by the customer?’” he told EE Times.

In quantum, that can mean helping system developers move from laboratory assemblies to reliable, reproducible equipment. Lozman cited 55 North’s investment in Monarch Quantum as an example: Optical modules that can be manufactured consistently become increasingly important as quantum companies professionalize their supply chains.

Lozman distinguished three types of quantum businesses, each with different commercial challenges and measures of progress:

  • Component suppliers: They must supply reliable, reproducible equipment as quantum computer builders scale production. Investors can examine revenue growth, production costs, and profitability. Lozman said he favors technologies serving multiple qubit architectures and several potential customers.
  • Quantum computer developers: They must move from demonstrating individual qubits to building useful, scalable systems. Investors assess their technical differentiation and approach to scaling, including whether they must build manufacturing capacity themselves or can use existing semiconductor infrastructure.
  • Software and applications companies: They must understand customer problems and prepare solutions for when suitable quantum hardware becomes available. Investors look for evidence of customer willingness to pay and a credible fit between the product and customer needs. Timing matters: Expanding before the hardware is ready can leave a company burning cash without sufficient revenue.

Value before revenue

Early sales provide evidence of demand, but they are not the only way a quantum company can become valuable. “In a lot of deep tech, the revenue is rarely the exit trigger,” Lozman said, referring to what prompts an acquisition or another opportunity for investors to cash out. “Technology is often the exit trigger.”

A system developer may lack a capability that a smaller company has developed. Bringing them together could create substantially more value than either business holds separately. Manaloto likewise sees value in defensible intellectual property, specialized engineering capabilities, strategic partnerships, and technologies that address critical industry bottlenecks—even before substantial revenue arrives.

Some companies pursuing complete quantum systems may ultimately merge or become component suppliers themselves, Lozman said. Their technology could remain important even if their original business model changes.

For applications companies, however, timing creates a particular danger. They need close customer relationships and a clear understanding of product requirements, but expanding before suitable hardware exists can leave them spending heavily without the expected revenue.

“If you’re a year or two early and you’re burning too much cash, it’s very, very difficult to sustain your company,” Lozman said. “Survivability will be a key kind of KPI for a lot of the assets in this space.”

Manaloto’s demand for intermediate products addresses that financing challenge. The objective is to build revenue and company value while progressing toward the final technology. But an intermediate product still needs a customer and a credible market.

Healthcare’s data opportunity

Healthcare is an application area that particularly interests Manaloto. His experience includes work with Kaiser Permanente’s innovation group and technology fund, where he encountered the difficulties of detecting disease earlier and obtaining useful biological information.

He sees opportunities in quantum sensing instruments that could reveal additional information about cellular processes. Unlike applications that depend on future quantum computers, some sensing businesses could commercialize instruments and measurements sooner, he argued.

Qubits Ventures has invested in Probius Bio, a Stanford spinout developing a quantum electrochemical spectroscopy platform. Manaloto described a system that captures molecular vibrational signatures from biological samples and converts those measurements into biochemical datasets that could support biomarker discovery, drug development, and biological research.

He is also evaluating an investment in an unnamed company developing diamond-based quantum sensing technology to investigate free radical activity and oxidative stress within living cells. Such measurements could help researchers and pharmaceutical companies study cellular behavior, disease mechanisms, and drug responses, he said.

For Manaloto, the opportunity extends beyond selling instruments. The greater potential lies in translating biological measurements that have been difficult to obtain into information that researchers, pharmaceutical companies, and eventually healthcare providers can act on. Research applications could provide an initial market before diagnostic or therapeutic uses are established.

“What do I do with that data? How do I translate it? How can pharma use it?” Manaloto said.

Those questions expose the distance between producing an unfamiliar measurement and delivering a useful product. A researcher needs to understand what the measurement reveals about the biological sample. A clinician needs evidence that it informs a decision. The technology must fit the way they already work—or offer enough benefit to persuade them to change their practices.

Integration with existing systems and compliance requirements add further work before a healthcare organization becomes a repeat customer, Manaloto said.

Capturing the benefit

Lozman identified another hurdle: The company selling a sensor may be separated from the organization receiving its greatest economic benefit. “It’s hard making money out of a sensor,” he said. “It’s hard to get people to recover the value if the buyer and the beneficiary are not close in the value chain.”

A measurement could improve a downstream process while leaving the instrument supplier struggling to capture a sufficient share of the benefit. The business model must connect the product’s price to an outcome the customer recognizes and will pay for.

In pharmaceutical research, Lozman sees potential opportunities in instruments that simplify drug discovery, improve toxicology assessment, or support better clinical-trial endpoints.

Qualification can be slow. Drawing on his experience across electronics and healthcare, Lozman noted that customers have strong reasons to protect processes that already work. A new technology must solve a sufficiently important problem to justify its introduction.

The same caution can benefit a company once its product is established. “Once you’re in, it’s very hard to get displaced,” Lozman said.

Both Manaloto and Lozman will attend the World Quantum Cannes Festival on November 17–18, where quantum technology providers, investors, and potential customers will meet to discuss applications and commercialization. For investors, those conversations offer an opportunity to hear how prospective users define their problems—and what they might be willing to pay to solve them.

For quantum investors, that’s where scientific promise must lead: a capability that solves a consequential problem, reaches the market at the right time, and gives its developer a defensible business. The roadmap to that outcome can matter as much as the eventual machine.

This week’s news of the $115 billion Marvell-Lumentum deal signals that silicon photonics has turned the corner from being discussed as a potential solution to the power wall caused by interconnect inefficiency to becoming a hotbed of activity, with an ecosystem ripe for exits that can help the technology scale and beat the limitations of copper in the evolving AI story.

Just two years ago, on the sidelines of the OFC conference in San Diego, I chaired a workshop panel discussing whether AI would be the killer application for silicon photonics.  At that time, we wrote, “It was clear from the presentations that we are at a potential turning point for silicon photonics. But there were still challenges in terms of scaling, energy efficiency, packaging, ecosystem, and tools like EDA and third-party IP, as well as materials.”

What we are seeing in the market today suggests that we’ve moved well beyond that point. It’s not just the large Marvell-Lumentum deal, but also the emergence of startups such as Salience Labs, which just raised $125 million in Series B funding to accelerate the deployment of its optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. Its backers include Applied Ventures, AMD Ventures, and Intel Capital.

You can watch our video interview with Salience Labs CEO and co-founder Vaysh Kewada here:

In this interview, we asked Kewada why she believes this is the right moment for optical switching and for Salience Labs, and how the company plans to achieve volume manufacturing and commercial adoption.  

She said that, by deliberately building its architecture on foundry processes capable of supporting volume production and aligning with co-packaged optics (CPO) manufacturing strategies early on, the company can mitigate standard supply chain friction. She added that 2027 will be a critical inflection year for volume production and deployment of its OCS technology.

Kewada told EE Times, “We’ve taken the approach of developing out an optical circuit switch that’s optical end-to-end so we’re never transforming the payload or the data into the electrical domain. The second differentiating standpoint is that we’ve chosen to take a fully integrated on-chip approach. And we’ve overcome the loss aspect of integrating optics onto the chip through the development of our own amplifiers that are also integrated on chip.”

In the same week that Salience Labs announced its funding round, another startup competing in the OCS space, Voyant Photonics, announced that it is developing a chip-scale OCS engine for AI data center networks. The company said it plans to deliver it to customers as a compact optical switching building block that can be integrated into next-generation data center switching platforms.

Voyant is not starting from scratch, though. It has already developed a high-density silicon photonics switch matrix to route light for its FMCW LiDAR systems. The architecture uses discrete, solid-state optical paths rather than moving mirrors or continuous analog beam steering. The company said this technology is now being adapted, since in a data center OCS implementation, it’s the same fundamental architecture that can be configured to route optical signals among communication ports.

Voyant plans to provide its OCS technology as an engine that optical networking companies can incorporate into their own platforms.  

The land grab for silicon photonics

In a report published last month, titled “The Interconnect Imperative—Why AI Is Forcing the Semiconductor Industry to Go Global”, Woodside Capital Partners wrote, “In the space of fifteen months, Marvell paid $3.54 billion for Celestial AI; Nvidia put $2 billion each into Coherent and Lumentum—and then $3.2 billion more into Corning; Ayar Labs closed a $650 million Series E at a $5.0 billion valuation; and Credo, Molex, GlobalFoundries, Ciena, AMD, and FormFactor each bought their way into a different layer of the stack.”

The authors added, “Our view is that this is a land grab for control points—lasers, optical engines, chiplets, packaging, test, and foundry capacity—and that it will not run forever. Each deal removes a control point from the board and raises the scarcity premium on what remains; but as the gaps fill, urgency will decline. For founders, the window for premium strategic exits is open now. For acquirers, the cost of waiting is compounding.”

This context helps explain Marvell’s interest in bringing Momentum into its already strong connectivity portfolio.

If you look at the silicon photonics landscape (see chart above), the ecosystem offers plenty of opportunities for partnerships, mergers, and acquisitions as companies race to beat that power wall.

As I stated in the Woodside Capital report, the surge in investment activity in silicon photonics, whether through high-ticket funding rounds or outright acquisitions, highlights a shift in which foundry economics are favorable to high-volume manufacturability and scaling. Over the past year, the industry has moved very quickly from viewing integrated silicon photonics as an emerging alternative to copper to recognizing optical interconnects as a viable physical backbone for scaling next-generation AI infrastructure.

data.title: STMicroelectronics Expands STM32 Roadmap for Cloud AI and Physical AI
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

STMicroelectronics is expanding its STM32 microcontroller (MCU) roadmap with multicore devices, hardware accelerators, and AI-assisted development tools as it positions the platform for growing cloud AI and physical AI markets.

“There are two rapidly growing markets today, cloud AI and physical AI, and it is our duty at ST to make sure that the STM32 platform will be the king of the microcontroller market in cloud AI and physical AI,” said Remi El-Ouazzane, president, microcontrollers, digital ICs, and RF products group at STMicroelectronics, answering a query posed by EE Times at ST’s global press briefing.

The company has introduced a unified STM32 microcontroller platform spanning industrial, automotive, and robotics applications.

Maria Erez, executive VP of STMicroelectronics’ embedded processing subgroup, said the unified STM32 platform is designed to let customers reuse existing software, development expertise, and manufacturing investments across product generations and application domains.

The company also announced its STM32A automotive and high-safety MCU portfolio, a new STM32G5 mixed-signal MCU series, a high-performance STM32H7P with a neural processing unit (NPU), redesigned edge AI development tools, and STM32Cube for agentic AI.

El-Ouazzane said the semiconductor industry is experiencing convergence across automotive, industrial, and other domains in areas such as AI, security, safety, connectivity, sensing, and control, creating opportunities to reuse common technologies and expertise.

“Across many applications, the challenge for customers and developers is shifting from selecting a single device to finding ways to reuse software, tools, architectures, and engineering expertise across multiple products and evolving requirements,” El-Ouazzane said.

“In other words, the value is shifting from the individual MCU to the broader platform surrounding it.”

The company sees this convergence extending to systems that can perceive, make decisions, and act autonomously in the physical world, including industrial equipment, automotive systems, and robots. While these applications share requirements for connectivity, real-time control, safety, security, and software lifecycle management, their specific certification requirements may differ.

Arm partnership

As part of its longstanding partnership with Arm, STMicroelectronics said it will help define the future Cortex-M processor roadmap, aiming to set up a common foundation for embedded systems.

The partnership also gives ST early access to Arm cores, allowing it to optimize its platform for the processor roadmap.

Erez said STM32 has helped drive Cortex-M adoption. STMicroelectronics said more than 100 billion devices use Arm Cortex-M cores. STMicroelectronics is working with more than 100 ecosystem companies through Arm’s Total Design program for physical AI, announced in September.

Arm said the program brings ecosystem partners together to accelerate development in the market, with STMicroelectronics and Cadence as key partners.

“Now, we want the entire industry to adopt it,” a company spokesperson said during the Q&A session, referring to the Cortex-M roadmap.

“The next major frontier for computing is bringing intelligence into the machines that move, manufacture, and operate in the physical world,” said Drew Henry, executive VP, physical AI at Arm.

STM32A for automotive and high-safety systems

The STM32A family extends the STM32 platform into automotive and high-safety systems. The first three devices are sampling to customers, and STMicroelectronics plans broader availability in 2027.

The STM32A4 targets entry-level automotive local control nodes and safety systems. The STM32A5 addresses mid-range safety-critical applications in industrial automation, robotics, and energy systems, as well as automotive applications. The STM32A9 addresses safety-critical, multi-domain control where real-time control, low latency, Ethernet, and deterministic communication are essential.

“This is about continuity,” Erez said. “STM32A is not a separate story. It is an extension of the STM32 platform strategy, which we plan to continue and expand.”

Both STM32 and STM32A will be supported by the STM32Cube ecosystem. Process technologies and intellectual property (IP) such as Cortex-M cores, timers, clock sources, analog components, and power management can be reused across domains. Safety certification requirements still differ by market. Industrial and automotive products must meet different functional safety standards and qualification requirements, with automotive applications commonly assessed under ISO 26262 and its Automotive Safety Integrity Levels (ASILs).

The company said future STM32 products will be built on its 40-nm flash technology and 18-nm fully depleted silicon-on-insulator (FD-SOI) technology with embedded phase-change memory, supplemented by TSMC’s embedded non-volatile memory (eNVM) technologies.

Erez said nearly 2 million unique developers use the STM32 ecosystem, and the number of active users has grown by around 20% over the past three years.

The company said customers choosing its Stellar automotive MCUs or STM32A have different application requirements. ST also sees more automotive companies moving into humanoid robotics, citing commonalities in functional safety and architecture. The company expects this trend to continue in the coming quarters and years.

STM32G5 for digital power and motor control

The STM32G5 series of mixed-signal MCUs is in production now. It uses an Arm Cortex-M33 core running at 280 MHz. ST said the series delivers twice the compute performance of the STM32G4 series.

The company targets the series for data centers, robotics, photovoltaic installations, wind turbines, industrial drives, and commercial drones.

“This new generation of microcontrollers addresses the challenge to meet the growing energy needs of AI data centers efficiently, realize more sophisticated humanoid robots, and power more complex motor-control systems,” said Patrick Aidoune, general manager, general purpose and automotive microcontrollers division at STMicroelectronics.

ST said GPU clusters are driving rack power toward 1 MW, and the largest data centers could demand more than 2 GW of peak power by 2030. The company said the STM32G5 is the first MCU with the company’s enhanced 12-channel high-resolution timer. Equipment makers can use it to reconfigure power supply units dynamically as server workloads change. The timer also lets the MCU handle the higher switching frequencies of power supplies built with silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN).

The company also said that robotics company Ruiyan Intelligent is using the STM32G5 in its next-generation robotic hands.

“In humanoid robotics, dexterity depends on combining strength, precision, sensing, and real-time control in an extremely compact space,” said Paul Tian, CEO of Ruiyan Intelligent.

The company said the series includes a programmable logic array, PLAy, which lets developers implement custom hardware functions on chip. Security features include Arm TrustZone, an immutable root of trust for secure boot and firmware updates, and support for ST’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) libraries. The device targets Platform Security Architecture (PSA) Level 3 certification.

STM32G5 devices offer 64 Kbytes to 512 Kbytes of on-chip flash, in packages from QFN32 to LQFP128. Prices start at $1.034 for orders of 10,000 pieces. ST plans to add dual-core products to the series in 2027.

Edge AI hardware and tools

The STM32H7P combines a Cortex-M7 core with ST’s proprietary NPU for AI processing. It will enter volume production in early 2027. Aidoune said one alpha customer working on solar inverters moved from managing arc-fault circuit breakers across four panels to 20 panels using a single MCU.

ST began rolling out new and redesigned edge AI tools at the end of October. These include Model Zoo for finding models, Model Factory for customizing and optimizing models, Dataset Factory for organizing datasets, and tools for basic model testing on ST boards. ST said it offers more than 400 pre-validated models and has supported more than 260,000 active projects with its AI tools over the past 12 months.

ST said deploying AI models on MCUs depends far more on development tools than on computing power.

STM32Cube for agentic AI gives AI agents access to STM32 knowledge, resources, and toolkits through a model context protocol (MCP) server. It provides validated reference code and STM32 code generation and review tools.

Aidoune said the tool complements STM32 Sidekick, ST’s AI-based technical support tool. “STM32 Sidekick helps answer developers’ technical questions, while STM32Cube for agentic AI integrates into the coding workflow itself,” he said.

El-Ouazzane said ST needs to strengthen its MCU portfolio with single-core and multicore devices, different security levels, and different types of accelerators, peripherals, and memory. “Today’s announcement of STM32Cube for agentic AI is a step in the right direction, but there is more we can do,” he said.

Ecosystem over compute

Responding to a question from EE Times China on whether the industry is heading toward a computing power race, ST said its ecosystem will be its biggest differentiator. The company expects multicore architectures to become a trend within the cost constraints of the microcontroller category.

The company defined physical AI as a subset of edge AI. Physical AI systems perceive, decide, and act in the physical world, with actual movement through components such as joints and actuators. It said this is where the convergence between automotive and industrial applications is strongest.

“The industry needs less fragmentation and a stronger focus on helping MCU technologies converge around a common foundation, while maximizing software reuse,” El-Ouazzane said.

data.title: Is There Room for Small-Scale OSATs in India’s Chip Packaging Boom?
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

India’s expanding outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) industry is creating opportunities for smaller, specialized packaging facilities alongside large, capital-intensive plants. Sahasra Semiconductors’ operating facility in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, represents one such entry point, with an investment of more than ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million), according to a May 2026 government announcement.

The question is whether smaller facilities can build commercially viable businesses by focusing on mature packaging technologies and specific product segments.

EE Times spoke with Nitin Dodia, semiconductor consultant and founder-director of Smart Fab Systems, who estimated that a facility focused on mature packaging technologies could be established with an investment of ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million). He said the amount would depend on the products handled, equipment requirements, and operating expenditure.

Dodia’s estimate applies mainly to mature, non-advanced products with simpler processes. “Simple wire bonding or leadframe-based packaging is less capital-intensive,” he said.

Production volume drives capital expenditure (capex), Dodia said. A company such as Micron processes millions of chips every month and needs equipment built for those volumes. OSATs handling specialized products with mature technologies can start with much lower capex.

Sahasra’s semiconductor packaging facility, set up under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s Scheme for Promotion of Manufacturing of Electronic Components and Semiconductors (SPECS), spans 5,295 square meters (57,000 square feet) and has a stated annual packaging capacity of 60 million units. It packages memory chips for microSD cards and flash storage, LED driver ICs, eSIMs, and RFID products. The government described Sahasra as India’s first small and medium enterprise (SME) to begin commercial production of semiconductor chips.

RRP Electronics operates an OSAT facility in Mahape, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, serving automotive, industrial, and telecom customers.

The larger OSATs work on a different scale. Tata Electronics’ ₹270 billion (~$3.25 billion) OSAT facility in Assam has an approved capacity of 48 million units a day. CG Power’s ₹76 billion (~$910 million) facility in Sanand, Gujarat, has a planned capacity of 15 million units a day. Kaynes Technology’s ₹33.07 billion (~$395 million) facility, also in Sanand, is designed to handle more than 6.33 million units a day. By comparison, Sahasra’s stated annual capacity of 60 million units translates into an average of about 164,000 units a day.

“The bigger point, however, is that success is not just about money,” Dodia said. “Whether you are setting up a smaller or a larger operation, you need to find an anchor customer.” He also pointed to capacity utilization, experienced personnel, and product qualification as key factors.

Customers before capital

Dodia said a new OSAT should secure at least one customer committed to buying its products over three to five years. This matters even more when the initial investment is low.

Companies such as Sahasra and RRP Electronics have an advantage because they entered the market earlier and already have customers buying their products. “That matters more than simply investing the money,” Dodia said. An investor could spend ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) on equipment. But if the equipment sits idle because no customers are lined up, the investment will not deliver the expected returns.

Larger players such as CG Semi and Kaynes Semicon follow the same model, with anchor customers and technology partners. Renesas, for example, is both a technology partner and an anchor customer for CG Semi, whose initial production serves Renesas’s packaging requirements. “Without that arrangement, there is little point in proceeding,” Dodia said.

Dodia said a buyer such as Apple or Samsung might have to work with 10 smaller OSATs, each with capacity tied to a ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) investment, to meet its requirements. “This creates additional management work for the customer as well,” he said.

Dodia said capacity utilization matters more than initial capex. Equipment is expensive whether a company invests ₹1 billion (~$11 million) or ₹10 billion (~$105.4 million). Idle equipment ties up money, and the company continues to pay interest. “Therefore, what matters most is whether your products and equipment are being utilized to their fullest potential,” he said.

Investors also need patience. Dodia said returns are typically zero in the first year, and investors should not expect returns in the first two or three years.

Experienced engineers are scarce

“In my view, the workforce, particularly experienced personnel, is the most underestimated requirement,” Dodia said.

Suppliers can provide quotes for equipment and material costs, he said, but experienced personnel is scarce worldwide. Indian OSATs compete for talent with the U.S. and other countries expanding chip manufacturing to reduce dependence on external suppliers.

Dodia expects the pool of experienced personnel to run dry. Much manufacturing knowledge is not documented. Two identical tools from the same vendor can behave differently over time as residue builds up in their process chambers. An experienced engineer can read statistical process control (SPC) charts and find the cause. AI cannot help without the data. “Most of the time, the knowledge exists in someone’s head,” Dodia said.

In an earlier interview with EE Times, Wasi Uddin, senior manager of R&D and training at Kaynes Semicon and a former OSAT and ATMP consultant at MeitY, said the “immediate gap is not materials or equipment; it is the expertise required to operate semiconductor-grade manufacturing facilities.” He said most of this expertise comes from the Philippines and Malaysia, or from Indian engineers who worked abroad and returned. Semiconductor manufacturers also have to compete with the IT sector on engineer salaries, he said.

A long road to qualification

Product qualification is the second hurdle, Dodia said. Qualification cycles often take 12 to 24 months, so a new OSAT cannot supply customers as soon as it installs equipment. A customer may ask for six or 12 consistent batches before it qualifies a supplier. Even then, the OSAT may serve only as a secondary supplier. Material suppliers can spend about 12 months qualifying with an OSAT.

Clusters versus a spread-out map

Dodia said smaller OSATs should ideally operate in clusters. Instead, states compete for semiconductor investment, and plants are spreading across the country. India has approved 12 projects under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). Dodia said a chemical supplier serving these plants and companies such as RRP Electronics may need warehouses in eight or 10 locations. Some materials, such as leadframes for certain relatively advanced packages, must come from within a few hundred kilometers of the OSAT because transport can affect them.

Tata has one plant in Dholera, Gujarat, and another in Assam, so its suppliers must manage logistics from west to east. Dodia acknowledged that states have reasons to share in the industry. But he said supply chains will take longer to mature. “Something that could have taken three years may now take five years,” he said.

Sanand in Gujarat shows the alternative. Dodia said Gujarat has three OSATs in Sanand and three more in the surrounding areas. One supplier facility nearby can serve three companies.

Uddin said that OSATs can import materials for the first three to five years while local suppliers build up. “Why is there no leadframe supplier till now in India? Because there was no OSAT, there was no market,” he said.

“Micron, CG Semi, and Kaynes formed a consortium and held monthly supplier meetings so suppliers could see their combined demand,” he said.

Room in legacy packaging

Commodity packaging puts smaller OSATs in competition with suppliers worldwide, Dodia said. Large OSATs, meanwhile, are directing their growth toward advanced packaging. Amkor’s advanced packaging revenue rose to $5.56 billion in 2025, while its mainstream wirebond business stayed flat at $1.15 billion.

Large OSATs also retire some older package lines. In 2022, ASE’s Chung-Li plant in Taiwan decommissioned its punch quad flat no-lead (QFN) line, forcing NXP to withdraw two parts.

Dodia sees an opportunity for smaller OSATs in these discontinued products. “Many products have such well-established applications that demand continues for 10 to 20 years. Automotive is one example,” he said. NXP has committed to supplying several automotive microcontroller families for more than 15 years, while Rohm Semiconductor specifies supply periods of 10 to 20 years for some products, including automotive MOSFETs.

He cautioned against crowding. If five or 10 smaller OSATs all target automotive, they will compete in the same race. “Ideally, they should coordinate their efforts, with one company targeting one segment and another focusing on a different segment,” he said. Some could pursue advanced packaging if they have the right customers, since startups and R&D teams often want newer technologies.

Uddin said the major OSAT players have already split by segment. Micron packages memory. CG Semi focuses on legacy packages such as QFN and thin shrink small outline packages (TSSOP). Kaynes focuses on power packaging, and Alpha and Omega Semiconductor has booked 28% of its capacity. “It will be a competition, that is for sure, but it will not be a throat-cutting kind of a competition,” he said.

Who will buy from smaller OSATs

Dodia said some customers pay a premium for dedicated capacity. Defense customers do not want their products exposed elsewhere and may pay more for a dedicated line. R&D teams and startups need small volumes quickly. When a larger manufacturer receives an order worth millions of dollars, a $10,000 order can wait for months. In all of these cases, time may matter more than unit cost.

Dodia said fabless startups are probably the best customers for new Indian OSATs. Serving them needs a flexible model that supports tens of processes, because their volumes are low and their requirements change fast. Integrated device manufacturers (IDMs) and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) companies could also become customers.

Global companies such as Renesas have two reasons to qualify a smaller Indian OSAT, Dodia said. Incentives could help it offer better prices. A dedicated partner also offers planned capacity for three to five years, without competing against the hundreds of customers that ASE or Amkor serve.

Dodia said India needs a tiered ecosystem, with large OSATs handling high volumes and smaller ones serving customers who need faster turnaround, greater security, or specialized services. Some mature markets abroad already follow this approach. If the ecosystem serves only high-volume customers, startups, defense customers, and R&D teams will not get what they need. “We definitely need both types of OSATs,” he said. Older products and mature technologies can meet many Indian requirements.

data.title: U.S. Manufacturing Activity Gains Momentum in October
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Economic activity in the U.S. manufacturing sector expanded for the 10th consecutive month in October, driven by accelerating production and steady growth in new factory orders. Sustained industrial activity helped buffer the broader economy against persistent commodity inflation, trade tariffs, and ongoing geopolitical tensions.

The Institute for Supply Management (ISM) reported that its Manufacturing Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) registered 55.5% in October, up 1.0 percentage point from September’s 54.5%.

The reading marks 10 straight months of industrial expansion after a 10-month contraction and indicates that the overall U.S. economy grew for a 24th consecutive month. According to ISM’s economic modeling, an October PMI reading of 55.5% corresponds to a 2.7% annualized increase in real gross domestic product (GDP).

“In October, U.S. manufacturing activity remained in expansion territory,” said Susan Spence, chair of the ISM Manufacturing Business Survey Committee. “Of the five subindexes that make up the PMI, four (New Orders, Production, Supplier Deliveries, and Inventories) grew faster than the previous month, while employment growth slowed down by 0.3 percentage points.”

Production hits multi-year high while new orders accelerate

Factory output expanded sharply during the month, as the Production Index climbed 2.3 percentage points to 59.0% in October from 56.7% in September. This represents the index’s highest reading since November 2021 (60.5%) and marks its 12th consecutive month of expansion.

Demand also picked up pace, with the New Orders Index reaching 55.5%, up 0.2 percentage points from September’s 55.3% for its 10th consecutive month of growth. Meanwhile, the Backlog of Orders Index fell to 54.6%, down 1.8 percentage points from September’s 56.4%, but remained in expansion for a 10th straight month.

Survey panelists in high-tech and defense markets emphasized strong demand alongside extreme lead-time pressure. “Explosive growth in the semiconductor and government/defense spaces has put us on our heels as we try to work through demand,” stated an executive in the machinery sector. “The long-awaited wave has arrived for our company, and it seems the global supply chain is in similar straits. Lead times and prices are rising, and some carry Covid-19 era delays—four weeks is now 50 weeks; a $2,000 item six months ago is now $4,000. We are hand-to-mouth. All the while, our customers are breaking down the doors complaining about our delivery delays.”

Another respondent in the miscellaneous manufacturing sector noted that AI infrastructure continues to squeeze commodity availability. “New month, same trends: Any commodity consumed by AI/data centers is in a crunch, both for supply and pricing,” the manager reported.

However, capital goods demand in non-AI sectors showed signs of hesitation. A computer and electronic products executive observed that “global demand for capital scientific instrumentation assets has slowed due to continued uncertainty in the Middle East, Eastern Europe, and China.”

The executive added that “anticipation over the mid-term elections and impact to funding for scientific research and the National Institutes of Health also is impacting customers’ purchasing behavior, making them focus on optimizing existing technology and tools.”

Payrolls expand for fourth month as inventories return to growth

Industrial employers continued to expand their workforce, although at a slightly moderated pace. The ISM Employment Index registered 52.4% in October, down 0.3 percentage points from September’s 52.7%, marking a fourth consecutive month of employment growth. Survey respondents favored hiring over headcount management by a 1.8-to-1 ratio.

Eight manufacturing industries reported expanding employment, with four of the big six sectors—Machinery, Transportation Equipment, Computer & Electronic Products, and Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products—posting hiring gains.

Raw materials inventories at manufacturing facilities returned to expansion territory after contracting in September. The Inventories Index jumped 2.8 percentage points to 51.4%, up from 48.6% in September. Seven industries expanded inventories in October, led by printing, plastics, textiles, and three of the big six sectors (Food, Beverage & Tobacco Products, Transportation Equipment, and Machinery).

Despite inventory rebuilds, manufacturers continued to voice concern over cost inflation and operational disruption. An executive in the chemical products sector reported that “costs are up more than 6%,” noting that “of the tracked items, only nine are lower, 24 are higher, and six are neutral.”

Price pressures soften slightly amid persistent trade and geopolitical friction

While raw material costs remained elevated, price inflation decelerated in October. The Prices Index registered 75.2%, down 2.7 percentage points from September’s 77.9%. Despite the decline, the index indicates that raw material prices increased for the 25th consecutive month, with 53.1% of respondents reporting higher prices compared to 58.6% in September. Five of the six largest manufacturing sectors reported paying higher input prices.

“The Prices Index reading is still being driven by (1) increases in steel and aluminum prices that impact the entire value chain, (2) tariffs applied to many imported goods, and (3) increases in petroleum-based products as a result of the Middle East conflict,” Spence explained.

Supply chain bottlenecks worsened slightly, with the Supplier Deliveries Index registering 59.1%, up 0.1 percentage point from September’s 59.0% and indicating slower delivery performance for the 11th consecutive month. Five of the six largest manufacturing industries reported slower deliveries.

Survey participants noted that tariffs and trade policies continued to impede business planning. A respondent from the primary metals sector pointed out, “Material shortages abound. Fuel remains high. Uncertainty remains constant.” The respondent added, “Canadian tariffs continue to have a negative impact on steel.” An executive in fabricated metal products concurred, stating that “economic policies coming out of Washington continue to weigh on business conditions” and that “Canadian tariffs continue to damage small U.S. businesses selling into that important market.”

Manufacturing weakness also showed signs of deepening in localized pockets. ISM reported that 6% of manufacturing GDP contracted in October, up from 2% in September. Furthermore, the share of sector GDP in strong contraction (defined as a composite PMI of 45% or lower) rose to 6%, up from 2% in September.

Spence noted that the share of sector GDP at or below 45% serves as “a good metric to gauge overall manufacturing weakness.”

data.title: Marvell Snaps Photonics Chipmaker Lumentum to Bolster AI Connectivity
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The AI networking specialist Nvidia’s Jensen Huang calls the next trillion-dollar company has made a long-anticipated move into photonics by acquiring optical component maker Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion. The two Nvidia-backed companies help move vast amounts of data between AI chips.

While Marvell offers solutions for electrical and optical interconnects, network switching, and XPU attach, Lumentum brings expertise in high-performance lasers, optical transceivers, optical circuit switching (OCS), and specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing. The combined company, bringing silicon and optics closer, aims to become a category leader in AI connectivity.

Industry watchers, long calling for a much closer co-design of electrical and optical technologies, have been hinting at deals like this since the early 2020s. They call it a fascinating move and a giant bet that the next generation of AI data will mostly run on light, not copper.

“AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation,” said Matt Murphy, chairman and CEO of Marvell. “We intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity,” he added.

What Marvell gets

It’s a hefty spend for Marvell. Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group, told Reuters this is an enormous bet, and investors are right to ask whether Marvell is paying too much and taking on too much at once. However, a closer look at this deal shows that Marvell is betting on steadily increasing demand for optical components, a critical but overlooked part of AI infrastructure.

In cloud computing, a major connectivity bottleneck is the hand‑off between silicon‑based NICs and laser‑driven transceivers. A tighter co-design across the electrical and optical signal chain could significantly reduce both latency and power draw. That’s what Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston calls a “$550 billion” market opportunity.

As optical connectivity moves closer to compute, the co-design of electrical and optical technologies could encompass the full signal path: silicon, lasers, packaging, and power efficiency. Marvell’s DSPs, switches, and custom accelerators sit inside data centers’ optical transceivers. On the other hand, Lumentum supplies the lasers for these optical transceivers, which convert electrical signals into light and back again.

With the Lumentum deal, Marvell gains access to laser chips that generate the light used in optical connections. Lumentum also offers optical circuit switches that redirect light without electrical conversion. Furthermore, the San Jose, California-based company brings advanced compound semiconductor manufacturing and process technologies, including indium phosphide (InP).

The lasers are a critical building block in near-packaged optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO) designs. The Lumentum acquisition will give Marvell greater control over lasers, a crucial component in the optical supply chain for AI connectivity infrastructure. Lumentum’s laser technology also complements Marvell’s optical interconnect ambitions; Marvell has recently acquired Celestial AI to bolster its optical interconnect offerings.

The tie-up of two AI connectivity suppliers could also help create a more vertically integrated AI networking portfolio and allow Marvell to compete more aggressively with Broadcom. Moreover, greater influence over a constrained part of the AI networking value chain could provide Marvell with a broader foundation for competing with Broadcom.

Timing isn’t everything here

While the tie-up between Marvell and Lumentum makes business sense, both companies’ shares dropped after the announcement. It’s one of the semiconductor industry’s largest takeovers, and it came at a time when investors are growing skittish about AI economics. The announcement came after a week of bruising tech sell-off.

But the convergence of connectivity semiconductors and photonics has long been on the cards. A coordinated alignment of networking chips, lasers, and other optical components could significantly reduce integration risks and shorten design engineers’ time to deployment. And that justifies the strategic rationale behind Marvell’s acquisition of optical component maker Lumentum.

It’s also worth mentioning that Nvidia backs both companies and invested $2 billion each in Marvell and Lumentum earlier this year. Marvell CEO Murphy calls this deal a double down on supporting Nvidia. He also shot down concerns about Nvidia’s circular dealmaking. “I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for Nvidia,” he said.
