data.title: Canada’s Quantum Sector Sets Sights on Commercialization
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Canada’s quantum sector has already demonstrated that it can produce world-class research, but the big question in 2026 is whether it can commercialize that research and translate it into strategic capabilities, sustainable companies, and technologies that customers can use.

The stakes extend beyond computing: Quantum sensing and communications are increasingly part of the conversation about sovereignty, while hardware developers face the engineering and financing challenges of building commercially useful quantum computers. Canada’s renewed defense focus offers a potential customer and development partner, but industry leaders want procurement, investment, and workforce development to move together.

The Canadian Quantum Champions Program, announced in December 2025, signaled that commitment. Its first phase provides up to C$92 million (~$64.5 million) in milestone-based contributions divided among Anyon Systems, Nord Quantique, Photonic, and Xanadu to advance scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computing. The new funding and benchmarking efforts are intended to help retain Canadian companies and intellectual property while testing their technical progress.

International attention is also growing around Canada’s quantum sector. Photonic, Xanadu, and Nord Quantique are participating in DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. The assessment of Canadian quantum architectures examines development roadmaps, scaling strategies, and costs—not simply qubit counts. The initiative aims to determine whether a system can deliver computational value that exceeds its cost by 2033.

Defense procurement presents path to adoption

Canada’s Defense Industrial Strategy identifies quantum sensing, communications, and computing as sovereign capabilities. At an Empire Club discussion earlier this year, military and industry leaders emphasized deployment and procurement, including the need to connect companies with operational problems rather than wait for fully mature technologies.

Released in 2023, Quantum 2030—the Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces’ quantum science and technology strategy implementation plan—sets out a roadmap for developing prototypes ready for field testing by 2030.

Julien Camirand Lemyre, CEO and co-founder of Sherbrooke-based Nord Quantique, sees defense as an adoption channel that can support earlier-stage development and create opportunities for Canadian suppliers. “How do we support earlier-stage-of-development technology that sometimes has been underfunded in Canada?” he asked. “I think [the Defense Industrial Strategy] is well-positioned to do just that.”

But purchasing equipment is only part of the task. “It is important for Canada to be prepared not only to buy quantum computers but also to use this technology,” he said.

That distinction matters because quantum technologies do not share one commercialization timetable. Julien Chosson, Canada quantum lead at IBM, describes quantum sensing as “probably the most mature technology,” while quantum computing has yet to translate into commercial applications. “It’s still part of the research path,” he said. Where defense can help computing, Chosson said, is by “helping build a stronger ecosystem. Until we have that, there is not much we’ll be able to develop for the defense sector on the quantum computing side.”

Jérôme Bourassa, CEO and co-founder of Sherbrooke-based Qubic Technologies, wants mission-focused programs for quantum sensing alongside support for computing. The Canadian Quantum Champions Program is “a good start,” he told EE Times. “I don’t think it’s enough, and I think I would like to see something similar but in other areas, so think about the defense-related technologies and quantum sensing in particular.”

Bourassa said companies need capital, closer ties with the Canadian Armed Forces, and government partners willing to tolerate technical risk. “Not everyone is going to win. Not everything is going to work.”

Qubic’s progress illustrates how procurement can bridge development and customer evaluation. In September, the company announced a federal contract worth up to C$1.5 million (~$1 million) to supply nine cryogenic amplifiers, along with components and software, for testing. The agreement follows its C$3.5 million (~$2.5 million) seed round in June and the sale of cryogenic amplifiers to Quantum Machines.

Capital meets the scaling challenge

For computing developers, commercial success depends on more than demonstrating quantum behavior. Error correction, cooling, connectivity, and manufacturing must come together at an economically workable scale.

Nord Quantique is tackling the overhead associated with quantum error correction. In most platforms, Camirand Lemyre said, error correction requires 100× to 1,000× more physical qubits. “This is how you end up with the need for a million qubits to get to a useful quantum computer.”

The company’s approach builds redundancy into individual bosonic qubits, aiming to reduce the additional hardware needed to protect quantum information. “What quantum error correction needs is not more qubits,” Camirand Lemyre said. “We need some form of redundancy.” Some competing systems will cost billions to build and will be the size of a data center, he said.

Camirand Lemyre specified that Nord Quantique’s goal is a useful system costing tens of millions of dollars and occupying a small room.

Qubic, which connects computing infrastructure with potential sensing and communications applications, addresses another constraint: extracting weak microwave signals without generating excessive noise or heat. Bourassa said Qubic’s superconducting amplifier is designed to dissipate roughly one ten-thousandth as much heat as conventional semiconductor amplifiers. Such semiconductor amplifiers can account for as much as half of a refrigerator’s cooling budget, he said.

He said reducing that heat load could free cooling capacity for additional qubits and improve the economics of superconducting systems. “If we can’t make a quantum computing infrastructure that is economically sound … it won’t happen,” Bourassa said.

In British Columbia, Photonic’s financing shows the scale of capital now assembling around quantum computing. The company’s final investment close in May expanded the round first announced in January to more than C$275 million (~$200 million) and brought its total capital raised to more than C$475 million (~$350 million). New participants included BDC, EDC, Bell Ventures, and InBC, alongside earlier investors including RBC, Telus, Microsoft, and BCI.

Photonic combines silicon spin qubits with optical connections in its Entanglement First architecture. Its strategy is to distribute quantum computation across interconnected modules, using connectivity to support scaling and efficient error correction. Its work with Telus also links quantum development to existing fiber infrastructure. These are pathways toward commercial-scale systems, not evidence that the end goal has already been reached.

Photonic’s latest proposal extends that scaling strategy into domestic manufacturing. Project Vanguard envisions a shared, multi-tenant semiconductor facility in Canada costing up to C$500 million (~$350.5 million) and serving quantum computing, AI, aerospace, defense, advanced sensing, and semiconductor packaging. Selected for the Canada Investment Summit Prospectus, the proposed facility is intended to help companies move from prototypes to production at home, retain greater control over intellectual property and supply chains, and build Canadian capacity in advanced fabrication, packaging, and technical workforce development.

Preparing users before the hardware arrives

Canada also needs organizations capable of identifying valuable problems, evaluating quantum approaches, and integrating them with classical computing.

Chosson said there is a difference between promising research and demonstrated commercial returns when it comes to IBM’s application development work: “We do not have an ROI yet. We do not have a demonstrated quantum advantage yet. We’re getting close and we have great research that’s very promising. It’s not been achieved yet.”

He said industry must bring economically relevant problems, while universities contribute expertise and train the people who will solve them. “Right now, the best way to do this is through industry-academia collaboration. All the talent is sitting in our academia, so we really need that collaboration to spark.”

The University of Saskatchewan’s acquisition of a quantum computer provides one model. Its open-architecture system combines a nine-qubit Rigetti processor with control and automation technology and a dilution refrigerator from Edmonton-based Zero Point Cryogenics. The university intends to connect the machine with expertise in vaccines, food security, energy, and other disciplines rather than treat it as an isolated quantum research tool.

Cloud access provides another route. CMC Microsystems’ Quantum Computing Sandbox, funded through the five-year, C$217 million (~$156 million) FABrIC program, combines supported access to quantum platforms with application expertise for Canadian researchers, startups, and small and midsized enterprises. The objective is to develop industry-relevant applications and practical experience without requiring every participant to build its own infrastructure.

In September, Quandela joined that effort through an agreement with CMC, adding a photonic computing option that includes access to a quantum processor located in Canada. The sandbox addresses an important adoption gap: Hardware access alone does not give users the expertise to judge where quantum computing might help.

Camirand Lemyre expects materials and molecular simulation to be among the first beneficiaries as useful hardware emerges. Nord Quantique is working with an OLED manufacturer interested in evaluating molecules before committing to laboratory testing. “It would be great if we could simulate those molecules before we actually have to spend all that time in the lab,” he said.

Chosson pointed to Canadian research in life sciences, energy, and finance while cautioning that these efforts remain exploratory.

Building a national quantum industry

The commercialization challenge also extends to Canada’s semiconductor sector.

FABrIC-backed photonics and quantum projects include Aeponyx’s development of low-loss silicon nitride photonic circuits for quantum applications under Pasqal’s ownership. Shared fabrication and packaging infrastructure can help turn specialized research into manufacturable components.

Rafal Janik, COO of Toronto-based Xanadu, argued that quantum investment also builds semiconductor capabilities through cleanrooms, tooling, packaging processes, and trained personnel. He sees those capabilities as valuable beyond any individual quantum architecture while calling for better national coordination to avoid duplicating work across institutions.

Coordination need not mean isolation. At UBC’s Stewart Blusson Quantum Matter Institute, quantum-materials research and international collaboration connect Canadian expertise with partners in Germany, Japan, and elsewhere.

Camirand Lemyre similarly rejects a single-hub approach. Sherbrooke, Waterloo, Toronto, and British Columbia contribute different strengths, and Canada needs to build not only a pipeline of early-stage companies but the workforce needed for production and engineering as the industry matures, he said. “Whoever builds a quantum computer that is useful is a global company. … It’s not about one single hub; it’s really about building a national champion.”

For Bourassa, the remaining gap is the investment required to retain the value of decades of Canadian research. “Now it’s a matter of how we make sure that we can create the best possible value from all the research investment that has been done over the past several decades in Canada and making sure that it is retained in Canada,” he said.

Government support has been good and instrumental, but Bourassa said it could be a lot better in the future as international competition intensifies. Commercialization requires a further commitment to companies, infrastructure, and talent, he added.

Camirand Lemyre echoed that concern: “We have not been a country that is known to take large risk on their companies.” Canada’s next test is whether its funding programs, procurement opportunities, and shared facilities can sustain that transition—not merely supporting discovery but also keeping the resulting capabilities and economic value at home.

data.title: Andes Waits For Market Momentum For Cuzco CPU

TAIPEI, Taiwan – Andes Technology has slowed development of its Cuzco high-end RISC-V CPU IP as it redirects engineering resources to a rapidly growing AI business, CTO Charlie Su told EE Times. Su insisted the project’s ambition remains, even if the technology emerges in a different form and on a different timeline than originally planned.

RISC-V IP vendor Andes had spun out Condor to develop Cuzco after identifying a future market need for a high-end data center CPU based on RISC-V, but pulled the technology back in-house earlier this year.

“The ecosystem needs to gradually go there before you have the hardware, otherwise you cannot catch the opportunity,” Su said. “We started, but as time went on, we found the AI part of our business continued to grow very strongly.”

Andes’s AI business currently accounts for half of its revenue, growing 30% last year and likely to grow 50% this year, Su said, which will require additional resources internally. Andes has a small deep learning accelerator (up to around 4 TOPS at 1 GHz) with its own compiler, but most of its revenue in AI comes from AI chip companies using Andes CPU cores for control, orchestration, and data movement (including Meta, d-Matrix, Fractile, and Axelera). Many of these licenses are for custom cores, and delivery schedules can be extremely demanding, Su said.

“We decided to consolidate and slow down [Cuzco], so we could put more resources on the immediate revenue generation part,” he said.

Once the need to reallocate resources emerged, Condor was an obvious target since Cuzco had not yet taken off commercially. The spinout received many inquiries after its launch at Hot Chips 2025, Su said, but these inquiries have been slow to convert to licenses.

“We could have put more effort into finishing Cuzco and maybe get one or two customers, but it’s not enough—we need to wait for bigger momentum,” he said. “So we decided to scale it back and move a little bit slower.”

Su also cited the rise of agentic AI in the early part of 2026 as a key driver for improving productivity and reducing headcount across the business this spring. Andes has its whole engineering team using AI agents to accelerate progress, with humans reviewing everything, Su said. Consolidating Condor was linked to this strategy.

Cuzco will still become a product, perhaps under another name, but the timeline has lengthened as Andes is working on it “slowly, while looking for signs we should speed up,” Su said. Winning in IP isn’t necessarily about getting to market first, he added; Andes’s embedded customers may use the same cores for 10 years or more, albeit on different process nodes.

“The core that brings us the most revenue today is one we designed more than 10 years ago,” Su said. “We want to do it right, make it reusable, instead of getting to market first.”

In the meantime, Andes’s experience with Cuzco can be leveraged within the company, while recent changes in Arm’s business model following its launch of high-end CPU silicon are positive for the IP giant’s competitors, including Andes, Su said.

“Arm changed its business model, and that has certainly affected customer trust, especially at the high end,” Su said. “[Embedded] customers also don’t know when it will hit their market.”

For now, high on Andes’s priority list is a main processor core for the storage market. The company already has 10 customers in production with smaller controller cores. It is also focusing on automotive and robotics.

“The bottom line is that the market Cuzco tried to address is still there and will continue, so that’s where we want to hit next in terms of our performance level,” Su said.

data.title: Google: Agentic AI Will Drive New Demands on Data Center CPUs
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

The requirements of agentic AI are placing new demands on data center CPUs and infrastructure as a whole, Mark Lohmeyer, vice president and general manager for AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, told EE Times.

“Chat is relatively straightforward—there’s a question and an answer, and it relies heavily on inference across GPUs or TPUs,” he said. “With agents, the nature of those interactions is changing quite a bit.”

With agents, the user’s high-level intent can be broken down into subtasks and assigned to a team of agents that can access other APIs, visit websites, write and run code—CPU tasks. Sessions can be much longer and can involve multiple human users, which means context and state need to be preserved over potentially days or weeks.

“Agents are often bursty, and often idle,” he said. “They don’t do anything for [say] a day or two until you come back to them, or maybe until some API responds… It’s unique from older CPU workloads, in that it needs to be stateful over a long period of time, but is often idle during that period of time, and then when it’s not idle, it’s highly bursty.”

Handling this in a performant and secure way is a big challenge the industry is facing today, Lohmeyer said.

“Demand is already very high and is growing rapidly,” he said. “So, how do we provide the infrastructure that can support that growth and do it cost-effectively?”

New workloads

Lohmeyer distinguished between the compute needed to run the agent itself, which is a new workload requiring new infrastructure, and other tasks such as accessing websites and APIs, which already existed but were previously interfacing with humans.

“Agentic workloads will have a meaningful impact on both of those elements,” he said.

Existing parts of the workload will grow dramatically since agents are much more demanding than humans and hundreds or thousands of agents can be brought online very quickly while the number of human users can’t grow as fast.

“Ideally, you’d like to have those agents and their context, the applications and data, relatively close to each other from a latency perspective, for performance reasons,” Lohmeyer said.

Locality is important, but enterprises will continue to be a distributed world, with most continuing to use multiple clouds and private clouds for the time being, Lohmeyer said. This means high-performance networks will also continue to be incredibly important both within the data center and between data centers.

“Dynamic, stateful agents will need to have a new type of computing infrastructure that supports them,” he said. “They’re accessing all the existing apps and data, so the demand there is growing, and all this needs to be connected together through the network. Google is investing in all of these elements.”

For the new infrastructure, the optimum ratio of CPU-to-GPU compute for agentic AI is still evolving with the workload, Lohmeyer said, but the proportion of CPU compute required is definitely increasing as we switch from training foundation models to agentic inference.

“We expect both [CPU and TPU/GPU] workloads to continue to grow rapidly, but the proportion of CPUs is going from a relatively small portion to a meaningful portion, and we think that will continue to evolve as agents expand into new use cases and new environments,” he said.

Hardware-software-workload co-design

Solving the agentic inference problem will continue to require co-design across the infrastructure stack, Lohmeyer said, including CPUs, storage, memory, networking, and how it all works together.

“Google Cloud has always had a philosophy of workload-optimized infrastructure,” he said. “This is more important than ever in the agentic era.”

Since agentic workloads are bursty and often leave the CPU idle, agents can effectively be “hibernated”—their state can be sent to storage so the CPU can be used by other agents, but reloaded quickly when required again.

“This requires a new type of orchestration in software, and in this environment, having really high-performance storage that’s attached to that server, so I can restart it quickly, is important,” he said.

Google Cloud uses microVMs, like a “slimmed down” version of a virtual machine, to provide a secure boundary between agents packed onto the same server. Rather than 100 traditional VMs, the same hardware might run 1,000 microVMs.

“Security and governance for agents is absolutely critical, and Google is investing a lot in every layer of the stack,” he said.

At the lowest layer, virtualization is key, Lohmeyer said. Google plans to support a variety of ways to sandbox agents, but the microVM is particularly important. A microVM’s streamlined feature set means performance is improved, and a smaller attack surface helps security, versus traditional virtual machines. The company is also investing in agent gateways that can provide egress controls for agents at the network level, along with other higher-level controls.

Looking forward, the requirement to run thousands of microVMs for agents will have implications for core density, storage, how storage is attached, and for orchestration software to manage it all, Lohmeyer said. The benefits will be higher utilization of hardware, which should drive down the cost per agent, he said.

“This will allow our customers to scale their business, but do so with a good business model, good profitability, but without having to sacrifice performance as they are scaling,” he said. “These capabilities will be very important going forward.”

CPU choice

There won’t be a single optimum CPU choice for every type of agent, Lohmeyer said. Google Cloud uses a variety of x86 CPUs from Intel and AMD as well as its in-house designed Axion CPU, which is Arm-based.

“If you’ve got a data-heavy agentic use case, maybe you need super high core performance and a large amount of local SSD, but maybe if it’s more web-serving, you just want a lot of cores,” he said. “We think that ultimately, customer choice and being able to map the specific agentic workload to the specific CPU option in Google Cloud will be important.”

There is “a lot of customer interest” in Axion at the moment, Lohmeyer said, across performance- and efficiency-optimized instances as well as interest for bare-metal instances from larger customers.

data.title: Intel’s Q3 Results Show Supply Chain Disruptions and PC Plunge
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Intel reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $16.5 billion, up 21% year over year, as expanded data center demand offset manufacturing bottlenecks and a sharp contraction in personal computer sales.

The results reflect a structural divide in the technology hardware sector. While AI infrastructure drives chip sales for server processors and memory suppliers, component shortages and elevated memory prices increase system costs and weigh on consumer hardware demand.

Data center demand collides with manufacturing bottlenecks

Intel’s Data Center and AI group generated $7.3 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 78% year over year, reflecting strong demand across hyperscale, enterprise, and cloud customers.

However, shortages of raw materials, substrates, and other critical components limited Intel’s ability to meet demand for its Xeon server family. A two-week shutdown at an Intel fabrication facility in Israel, following a gas explosion, further impacted production.

Because turning silicon wafers into finished chips takes roughly three months, wafers that were still in process when the fab shut down will likely be scrapped. Intel CFO David Zinsner said during the earnings call most of those write-offs should land in the fourth quarter, and he does not expect further scrapping in the first quarter. He said the fab disruption will have an estimated $300 million impact on revenue in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a similar impact in the first quarter of 2027.

“Our Q3 results demonstrate improving execution, meaningful progress expanding supply and continued advancement of our process technology,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said in the press release. 

“I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Tan said in the earnings call. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing supply shortage, the unprecedented memory crunch, and the resulting softness in PC demand. But I remain confident in our path forward.”

The company projected fourth-quarter revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion and a non-GAAP gross margin of 38.0%, down from 44.1% in the third quarter.

Memory shortage and PC market contraction

While Intel struggled with component supply, memory manufacturers benefited from rising demand driven by AI infrastructure investment. Both Samsung and SK Hynix recently reported record quarterly profits.

Rising memory prices created direct headwinds for personal computer manufacturers and Intel’s Client Computing and Physical AI Group, where revenue declined 5% year over year to $8.1 billion. 

Surging DRAM costs from vendors including Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron forced PC makers to raise retail prices, prompting buyers to defer upgrades. “We expect the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize,” said Tan during the earnings call. “While the next few quarters will be challenging for the PC market, our roadmap continues to strengthen, and our long-term outlook remains positive.”

Industry adjustment and outlook

Data from Counterpoint Research indicates that global personal computer shipments fell 21% year over year in the third quarter of 2026 to 57 million units. The firm forecasts a further 27% year-over-year decline in the fourth quarter. 

Minsoo Kang, a senior analyst at Counterpoint Research, noted in a report, “The global PC market is facing mounting pressure as rising memory and component costs push system prices higher and force consumers to delay replacement purchases.”

Analyst commentary underscores how high component pricing affects hardware purchasing patterns across the supply chain. David Naranjo, associate director at Counterpoint Research, stated: “The PC industry is entering a period of structural adjustment, where rising component costs, higher system prices, and longer replacement cycles are fundamentally reshaping market dynamics.”

Zinsner said Intel does not expect to generate positive free cash flow in 2027, which he described as an “investment year”. The group plans to increase capital expenditure to rebuild production capacity.

data.title: Infineon’s OktoberTech: Edge AI, SDVs, and the Road to 800 VDC
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Infineon held its 10th annual OktoberTech event on Oct. 22 at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California. While touring the museum’s exhibits, participants could attend several executive briefings focused primarily on physical AI, with sessions on robotics, automotive, and power systems. 

Between the executive briefings and keynotes, theoretical physicist, City College of New York professor, and best-selling author Michio Kaku gave a talk on the waves of innovation (Figure 1). The idea is closely associated with economist Joseph Schumpeter, whose theory of creative destruction states that new inventions render older ones obsolete.

Kaku traced these waves from steam power during the Industrial Revolution, through the transistor and the Information Age, to today’s AI revolution. He then looked ahead to how quantum computing, brain-computer interfaces (BCIs), and other advances could give rise to entirely new industries and transform life as we know it. As with many of Kaku’s talks, it was a thought-provoking glimpse into what the future could hold at our current pace of technological advancement.

Semiconductors at the center

Infineon’s OktoberTech event covered automotive semiconductors, power electronics, and embedded processing, with discussions highlighting the growing demands that AI infrastructure places on semiconductor technologies and manufacturing capacity.

Edge AI, IoT, and now physical AI: What’s different now?

The journalists asked about the initial hype around IoT, edge computing, and software-defined vehicles (SDVs).

IoT, for example, was all the rage for a while, when everyone expected every device to be wirelessly connected and streaming monitoring data to the cloud. One journalist pointed out that the billions of connected devices once promised over cellular, Wi-Fi, and low-power networks never materialized, and that IoT conferences that once drew 12,000 to 14,000 in Silicon Valley no longer exist. So why should the industry believe that edge AI will be any different?

Stefan Zizala, division president of edge systems at Infineon, who took the question, called IoT “an unfulfilled promise” rather than a failure. The difference now, he argued, is that more capable microcontrollers with more memory can run AI models locally. “Not every piece of information needs to be fed back to the cloud,” Zizala said. “I think that’s the big difference…they are processed with AI right at the edge…and the results are then sent back to the cloud…So, it’s a conceptual change.”

Zizala said the change is already visible in everyday devices such as power tools and home appliances. In his session, he added that machine-learning algorithms are now used in electric motor control for predictive maintenance and gave further reasons to keep processing local: the cost of cloud tokens, lack of connectivity, latency, and data protection.

SDVs

SDVs were another example. According to Peter Schiefer, president and CEO of the Automotive Division at Infineon, only about 10% of vehicles have a software-defined architecture today, leaving roughly 90% without one. He predicted that share would climb to around 40%. Audience members suggested that newcomers, particularly in China, have the advantage because they can design vehicles from a “clean sheet of paper” without legacy architectures. Schiefer agreed that greenfield companies have an easier path.

Schiefer also pointed to another setback: Western OEMs had tied their SDV launches to new EV platforms, so when those platforms were canceled, SDV rollouts were delayed as well. China, by contrast, has reached about 50% EV penetration, which has given Chinese automakers a competitive edge. His conclusion was that legacy OEMs can only manage the growing complexity by controlling their own software. That means consolidating the roughly 100 distributed control boxes, each with its own dedicated software, into a central computer. “That’s the only way traditional OEMs can survive. And I think meanwhile they recognize it, and they need to catch up,” Schiefer said.

Data center power and the Dresden fab

While most of the event centered on physical AI, the power systems executive briefing focused more on power requirements for data centers.

Infineon released a litany of data center-related news in October, including its 27 kW three-phase PSU reference design, the 800 VDC and ±400 V digital hot-swap controller, the first 900-V GaN bidirectional switch (BDS) to be used in Enphase’s IQ solid-state transformer (SST), and the 800 V to 50 V, 12 V, 6 V GaN intermediate bus converter (IBC) collaboration with Nvidia.

That investment in data center power extends to manufacturing. In July, Infineon opened its €5 billion (~$5.58 billion) Smart Power Fab in Dresden, a 300-mm facility for power and analog/mixed-signal devices and the largest single investment in the company’s history. Adam White, president of Infineon’s Power and Sensor Systems division, pitched it to the room as capacity ready for the AI buildout (Figure 2): “This facility is at the moment empty, okay? But I promise you now, with the demand that we’re seeing, that facility will be ramped.” He added that the fab is “open there for the industry.” Full production is set to ramp up in late 2026.

On when 800 V DC would reach the market, White said, “We may start seeing some of the first, whether they’re prototypes or mass productions, definitely in ‘28.” He framed it as the end state of a longer path, from single-phase to three-phase and ultimately from high-voltage AC to medium-voltage DC at the facility level, i.e., “the holy grail to get to the 1 MW rack.” That diverges from today’s sidecar approach, in which 800 V is produced locally from three-phase AC. He also cautioned that significant barriers to entry remain, as the industry must maintain UL certification and safety from the get-go.

IBCs

On the topic of IBCs, Infineon released the 800-to-50 V and 800-to-12 V IBCs in March 2026, both using 650-V CoolGaN on the primary side (Table 1).

Table 1: Specifications of Infineon’s 800 V-to-50 V and 800 V-to-12 V CoolGaN IBC reference designs

The October release reinforces the role of GaN in IBCs, an approach also pursued by other power vendors (e.g., Renesas, TI, ST, Navitas, etc.). It also confirms that Infineon is actively developing IBCs for 800-to-6 V conversion. These IBCs take 800 VDC from the sidecar and convert it closer to the core, potentially leaving room for power converters to take the 6 V directly to the sub-1V core voltages (though there is room for debate here).

The physics are clear: I²R losses dominate as voltage drops and current rises. The 20 kW-class 800-to-6 V converters shown at GTC 2026 push more than 3,000 A at their output (20 kW / 6 V ≈ 3,300 A). The closer you get to core voltage, the shorter the electrical path to the xPU must be, which is what has driven the need for VPD on AI processors, namely GPUs.

Discussing power delivery to various xPUs (GPUs, CPUs, TPUs, etc.), a panelist noted that lateral power delivery (LPD) will remain applicable for CPU-heavy agentic racks. While the GPU remains the dominant processor for training with an 8:1 GPU-CPU ratio, inference (~4:1) and agentic (~1:1) workloads shift that ratio more favorably toward CPUs [2]. “From the customer interactions that we’re having, there are clear commitments I see from some of the bigger companies to go down to a ratio of 1:1,” White said. “Of course, that’s a dramatic change from 8:1 ratios that were there previously.”

Samsung Electronics reported third-quarter consolidated revenue of 195.3 trillion won (~$146 billion) and operating profit of 107.4 trillion won (~$80 billion). Strong global demand for AI memory chips underpinned the results.

Samsung said it is the first technology company globally to exceed 100 trillion won (~$75 billion) in quarterly operating profit, illustrating how AI infrastructure spending drives hardware economics across global supply chains.

However, rising component prices weighed on Samsung’s mobile business, while its shareholder return plans fell short of investor expectations.

Financial split between chips and consumer devices

The earnings report highlighted a stark contrast between Samsung’s component manufacturing and finished consumer electronics. The Device Solutions (DS) semiconductor division generated 147.1 trillion won (~$110 billion) in revenue and 106.5 trillion won (~$80 billion) in operating profit. In contrast, the Device eXperience (DX) division, which includes smartphones, televisions, and home appliances, posted an operating loss of 0.8 trillion won (~$0.6 billion) on revenue of 52.1 trillion won (~$39 billion).

“Another record-breaking quarter, beating consensus estimates,” said MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint Research, noting that semiconductor operating profit surpassed 100 trillion won (~$75 billion) while finished consumer set divisions slipped into an operating loss.

Memory pricing and supply chain adjustment

Memory pricing helped drive the divergence between Samsung’s semiconductor and consumer device businesses. Counterpoint Research argued that standard DRAM pricing rose from the historical range of 20-30 cents per gigabit to $2 per gigabit, expanding the global DRAM market to $200 billion. Samsung reported operating margins of 79% for DRAM and 72% for NAND flash. Meanwhile, as the high-bandwidth memory market (HBM) grows, HBM4 prices are expected to reach $4 per gigabit. 

Higher memory prices put pressure on bill-of-materials across mobile manufacturing. Samsung’s Mobile eXperience (MX) and Networks business generated 37.7 trillion won (~$28.21 billion) in revenue but posted an operating loss of 0.6 trillion won (~$0.45 billion).

“The [consumer electronics] MX division continues to suffer from high memory pricing,” Hwang said. “Since low-end models are expected to continue losing money, Samsung may scale back its volume contribution, implying further correction in market volume dynamics in the supply chain.”

In the presentation before the earnings call, Samsung Mobile VP Daniel Araujo noted that the business aims to “mitigate profitability risks through efficiency improvements” and “improve our product mix centered on flagships.”

HBM expansion

Samsung’s results are consistent with those reported by SK Hynix, which posted third-quarter revenue of 104.62 trillion won (~$78 billion) and operating profit of 83.33 trillion won (~$62 billion).

The company said “it significantly scaled up sales of HBM4” on the back of product competitiveness while managing its “product mix, with focus on AI products, amid capacity constraints.”

During the earnings call, Jaejune Kim, EVP of Memory Business at Samsung Electronics, said the company has secured multi-year supply agreements with 10 key customers. However, while competitor SK Hynix stated that its HBM capacity is fully sold out through 2029, Samsung confirmed its HBM capacity is currently sold out through 2027.

Counterpoint Research expects Samsung to gain ground in advanced memory. “We anticipate that Samsung will surpass SK Hynix from the HBM4 generation, leading the market share in 2027,” Hwang said on SK Hynix results.

Capital allocation fuels investor pressure

Despite high operating income, Samsung’s share price fell during the earnings call as the capital allocation plan met expectations. The company announced a third-quarter cash dividend of 30 trillion won (~$22 billion) as part of an estimated total shareholder return plan of 90 trillion won (~$67 billion) to 110 trillion won (~$82 billion) for 2026.

Samsung CFO Soon-Cheol Park highlighted that long-term capital deployment will remain aligned with industry expansion, noting that “memory demand will far exceed supply due to robust AI investment” and “AI infrastructure investment continues to grow”.

“Shares declined during the earnings announcement as shareholder returns offered no upside surprise,” Hwang concluded, pointing out that the market reaction “highlights the real challenge of navigating an equity market with elevated expectations.”

data.title: STMicroelectronics Weighs Developing More Powerful MCUs, MPUs for Humanoid Robots
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

STMicroelectronics argued that humanoid robots should use onboard sensors and cameras to handle fast reactions on the robot, and leave only whole-body coordination to a central GPU, because a round trip to the GPU adds latency a moving robot cannot afford. The chipmaker is still weighing whether to build more powerful MCUs or MPUs for the task, a decision it says depends on how the robotics market develops.

“Every millisecond counts,” Allan Lagasca, director of STMicroelectronics’ robotics segment strategic program, told EE Times. “If you want a fast reaction, you should move the processing to the edge. If you want the entire system to work together, that is where the GPU comes in.”

Running inference closer to the task can reduce the workload sent to a central GPU and avoid delays associated with transferring data and returning commands, Lagasca said. In robotics, those delays can affect physical movement.

When two hands coordinate to transfer an object, for example, a delayed command can cause a joint to miss its target. Even if individual joints miss their targets by only a few millimeters, the combined movement can be affected.

“If inference is performed at the edge, the system can send the necessary command locally and respond faster,” he said.

The central GPU, which Lagasca called the robot’s “larger brain,” still has to synchronize the head cameras, machine vision, and navigation, and coordinate joints whose sensors are not connected to one another. Without that coordination, he said, “the robot could move both feet forward at the wrong time.” STMicroelectronics does not make GPUs.

The chipmaker’s current AI inference products are based on its neural processing unit (NPU) and microprocessor unit (MPU), Lagasca said. Whether it develops more powerful chips depends on how the market evolves.

Robotics is still a low-volume market, while STMicroelectronics, as an integrated device manufacturer, targets high-volume production. “By following this market, we will better understand which technologies are needed,” he said.

Where the hand does its own thinking

In a robotic hand demonstration at electronica India, a camera captured an image of a human hand, and an AI model identified 21 points to recognize the gesture. The system then translated that information into commands for a robotic hand with six motors. Gesture recognition ran on STMicroelectronics’ STM32N6 32-bit microcontroller.

“The mapping is not simple,” Lagasca said. “It is not even a one-to-one or one-to-two relationship, and it must run continuously as the hand moves.”

The work starts with the camera. Its module combines an image sensor to capture images, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) to determine the camera’s position and orientation, and a time-of-flight (ToF) sensor to measure distance. “Capturing an image is not enough; you also need to measure the distance,” Lagasca said. The ToF reading tells the hand when to close its fingers.

Inference also runs mainly onboard the camera, partly for privacy, Lagasca said. As long as an image is used for inference without being stored or sent elsewhere, the system can meet privacy and cybersecurity requirements, he added.

The camera’s output then has to be translated into commands the motors can use. Lagasca said the gesture recognition demonstration used a standard PLC to bridge AI outputs and robotic control. “The difficulty lies in translating the data generated by AI into a format that can be transferred to a standard PLC to control the robot,” he said.

The same edge approach enables the hand to adjust its grip. Humans adjust their hold on a water bottle almost instinctively; a robot has to compute the required grip.

In another example, Lagasca described a hand that identifies a water bottle, determines its distance, and adjusts its grip to avoid crushing it or letting it slip. “The MCU, in this case the STM32, performs this inference,” he said.

Each part of the robot handles its share. Most sensors have their own MCUs, Lagasca said, as do the motion and motor-control functions, while AI inference has its own NPU. “This creates a distributed architecture rather than putting everything into a single processor,” he said.

Integrating robotic modules and simplifying hardware

Humanoid robot manufacturers may source hands, joints, and cameras from different suppliers. Integrating these components can create problems with camera placement, board space, and motor control. A camera mounted on top of a hand may require the robot to reposition its hand before lifting an object, while one mounted underneath may strike the table during pickup.

STMicroelectronics said it is exploring ways to integrate camera technology and other functions into the humanoid hand itself. Although the company does not manufacture camera modules, it can combine its technologies with those of its partners. Earlier this year, STMicroelectronics and camera-module maker Leopard Imaging introduced a multimodal vision module for humanoid robots that combines STMicroelectronics’ imaging technology, 3D depth-mapping, and motion sensors. The module connects over Ethernet through Nvidia’s Holoscan Sensor Bridge to Nvidia’s Jetson computers and Isaac robot development platform. It is designed to fit the size, weight, and power limits of humanoid robots.

Lagasca said the broader approach is to divide the robot into modules, including hands, joints, feet, and eyes, that can be adapted to different applications and form factors.

Packaging the required functions within these modules presents another challenge. Designers must fit processing, motor control, and connectivity into the available board space. Lagasca cited a customer requirement for a 6 × 6-centimeter board.

Choosing MCUs, motor drivers, and connectivity parts separately could produce a design measuring 140 × 330 mm, far larger than the board, he said. For its robotic hand, ST integrated six MOSFETs and three drivers into one package, so a manufacturer can mount one part instead of nine.

Safety remains an open question

The distribution of intelligence across a robot also raises safety concerns. Lagasca said existing safety frameworks include Safety Integrity Level (SIL) requirements for industrial applications and Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL) requirements in the automotive sector. These requirements may become relevant as companies from the automotive, industrial automation, smartphone, and home appliance markets enter robotics.

However, compliance with a standard doesn’t guarantee that the entire robot is safe.

“If a sensor fails, the robot could still cause an injury, even if it meets the relevant SIL or ASIL standard,” Lagasca said.

AI can introduce additional risks if a system fails to make a decision or makes the wrong one, he said. All these elements must be considered together to assess a robot’s functional safety.

Lagasca added that many existing standards were developed for fixed equipment rather than moving robots. The industry still needs to determine which standards and regulatory requirements are appropriate for humanoid systems, particularly those that interact directly with people.

The chipmaker’s role in the humanoid bill of materials

Lagasca said that STMicroelectronics can address approximately 600 positions in a humanoid robot’s bill of materials (BOM), covering more than 500 components. The share of a robot’s total cost that this represents depends on its design, including how many joints, sensors, and AI functions the robot has, he added.

As an illustration, he said that if a robot’s BOM were worth $600 and STMicroelectronics supplied all of it, the chipmaker’s share would be 100%. If the BOM grew to $1,000 while the chipmaker’s parts remained valued at $600, its share would fall to 60%.

Entry-level robots may cost less and have fewer degrees of freedom, while mid-range and high-end systems may require more sophisticated capabilities. Depending on the design, Lagasca said STMicroelectronics could potentially address 800 or more positions as the number of joints, sensors, cameras, and AI-processing requirements increases.

From demonstrations to deployment

Despite the growing number of humanoid robot demonstrations, Lagasca said many applications remain at the proof-of-concept stage. Automotive manufacturing and logistics are among the early areas of interest because manufacturers can justify the cost of automation and adjust production lines to meet market demand.

He cited Boston Dynamics’ association with Hyundai and Figure AI’s relationship with BMW as examples of links between humanoid robotics and the automotive industry. Hyundai, which owns Boston Dynamics, plans to start deploying Atlas robots at its Georgia plant in 2028, while BMW has conducted trials for Figure robots in its Spartanburg, S.C., body shop.

Moving beyond demonstrations presents several challenges. Training data is one of them. Activities such as drilling, soldering, cooking, and sewing can be recorded and uploaded to create datasets, Lagasca said.

Battery technology doesn’t yet support 24-hour operation, he said, making downtime a practical consideration for developers.

The applications that reach the market will also depend on safety and regulatory requirements. Lagasca said direct physical interaction between humanoid robots and people presents additional challenges, particularly in healthcare.

Cybersecurity is another concern. Lagasca said that chipmakers and device manufacturers must account for the EU Cyber Resilience Act and other applicable requirements at both the product and application levels. “You do not want 10,000 robots operating in the real world only for someone to hack into them,” he said.

How intelligence is ultimately distributed between the edge processors and the central GPU may depend on a question the industry has not settled: What a humanoid robot should look like. The system architecture “has not stabilized,” Lagasca said. “Some developers ask why a robot should have only two hands rather than six, or only two legs.”

“We do not yet know what the final configuration will be,” he said.

data.title: Canadian Startup Aims to Be Quantum’s ‘Picks’ and ‘Shovels’
data.description:

There’s no shortage of hurdles that need to be overcome to scale quantum computing into a commercial reality. Canadian startup Meissner Technologies has focused on a critical bottleneck: superconducting materials used in single-photon detectors. 

Founded in September 2025 by University of Toronto materials science graduate Olivia Leng, Meissner Technologies uses AI, machine-learning simulations, chemical and electrical simulations, and laboratory testing to discover new superconducting materials in quantum computing. The company is also exploring materials that could reduce cooling requirements for photonic quantum systems. 

The Meissner team is largely drawn from the University of Toronto. The company has completed the Creative Destruction Lab program, a nonprofit objectives-based mentorship program for pre-seed and seed-stage deep-tech startups building massively scalable products and services. 

Meissner also recently closed its first financing round, anchored by the BDC Thrive Venture Fund, with backing from founders, operators, and investors including Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO of Xanadu. 

Leng’s path to entrepreneurship began during her studies, when she worked extensively with superconducting materials in both research labs and simulation environments. “I spent a lot of time in the lab, ran a bunch of simulation work on them, and noticed that there has been a lot of momentum going into the AI for drug discovery space,” she said. 

Leng realized that a similar framework and approach could be applied to finding new superconducting materials. 

Although photonic systems operate largely at room temperature, they still rely on single-photon detectors that must be cooled to extremely low temperatures. 

Current detectors typically use niobium titanium nitride or niobium nitride. According to Leng, those materials impose an unavoidable tradeoff between operating temperature and detector performance. 

Meissner said it believes better materials could significantly change the economics of quantum computing infrastructure. 

The company is searching for alternatives capable of operating a few degrees warmer than current options without compromising performance. While that may sound like a marginal improvement, Leng argued that the impact could be dramatic. 

“If we’re able to remove the dilution refrigerators, we’d be able to replace them with closed-loop helium-4 cryostats, saving them up to 95% of their cooling costs,” she said. 

The challenge is becoming increasingly urgent because of the industry’s dependence on helium-3. Leng noted that limited global supplies could eventually constrain scaling across multiple quantum computing platforms. 

That focus immediately resonated with investors and industry participants, she said. “We want to be the picks and shovels to quantum computing. That’s where we think a large part of the value chain can be captured.” 

With fresh funding secured, Meissner is moving from computational discovery into experimental validation. For several months, the company concentrated on refining its simulation stack. It is now advancing promising material candidates into fabrication and testing. 

“We’re actually depositing them into thin films, etching them into nanowires, and packaging them into photon detectors and running actual lab tests,” Leng said. “Then we take that lab data and feed that back into our model, creating this circular materials discovery pipeline.” 

The next major milestone is to deliver a minimum viable photon detector that can be piloted with a photonic quantum computing customer. A seed financing round is expected next year, with future investment directed toward detector manufacturing scale-up. 

Beyond that, the company has a more ambitious vision: autonomous materials research. 

“Our largest bottleneck right now is experimental validation,” Leng said. “We’re able to pump out so many candidates computationally, but we only have so much manpower.” Meissner ultimately aims to build self-driving laboratories capable of automating much of the materials discovery workflow, she added. 

Leng also sees Canada as an increasingly attractive place to build a quantum technology company. She pointed to support from ecosystems in Toronto, Waterloo, and Sherbrooke, along with a growing base of talent and investors. 

“I think our ecosystem has advanced to the point where it’s far more viable to build a company here in Canada, and we intend to stay Canadian,” she said. 

Internationally, Meissner faces established detector suppliers such as ID Quantique and Single Quantum. However, Leng argued that those firms are primarily improving detector performance through engineering refinements, while Meissner is focused on discovering entirely new materials. 

“Our hypothesis is [that] niobium titanium nitride has been around for decades in academia,” she said. “Every sort of variation has been exhausted. The only way to really improve detector performance meaningfully is to actually go in and investigate the materials science.” 

The company’s technology roadmap could also reach beyond quantum computing. Leng cited opportunities in quantum communications, aerospace sensing applications, and nuclear fusion, all of which depend on advanced superconducting materials. 

“Ultimately, we’re a materials discovery company,” she said. “We’re not going to just be bounded by quantum computing.”

SK Hynix posted third-quarter revenue of 104.62 trillion won (~$78 billion), exceeding 100 trillion won (~$75 billion) for the first time. Operating profit reached a record 83.33 trillion won ($62 billion), with an operating margin of 80%. Net profit was 39.78 trillion won ($30 billion), while net cash expanded to 98.7 trillion won (~$74 billion).

“SK Hynix’s third-quarter results are very significant in terms of hitting record-high earnings and delivering on shareholder value,” MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint Research, noted. “First and foremost, operating profit beat expectations again, coming in at 83 trillion won [~$62 billion] versus the consensus of 77 trillion won [~$57 billion].”

DRAM pricing jumps to $2/Gb

According to Counterpoint Research, standard DRAM pricing surged from 20 cents to 30 cents per Gb to $2 per Gb, driving financial momentum and expanding the global DRAM market to $200 billion. “The driving force behind this is rising prices,” Hwang said. “Prices that used to sit around 20 to 30 cents per Gb have now soared to $2.” He also argued that HBM4 will see its unit price jump even further to $4 per Gb.

Additionally, Nvidia resolved initial HBM4 bottlenecks. “Over the past few months, the market has been plagued by two major misconceptions and concerns regarding HBM: That SK was facing technical hurdles in supplying HBM4 to Nvidia, and that HBM adoption volumes per chip might decrease,” he added. “As of October, both concerns have proven to be fake alarms or have been largely resolved.”

Supply shortage and long-term agreements

As AI expands into enterprise computing, robotics, and autonomous vehicles, SK Hynix projects a structural memory shortage that will persist through 2030. The issue stems from the manufacturing complexity of 10 nm-class, sixth-generation DRAM, and 321-layer NAND.

To secure revenue, SK Hynix said it has signed long-term agreements (LTAs) with 14 tech giants, covering over 50% of capacity for 2027 to 2028. “Today, more than half of the memory industry’s capital expenditure goes into infrastructure,” Hwang said. “This shift in corporate governance leading to stricter capital discipline could ultimately rewrite the traditional memory business cycle.”

Solidigm IPO canceled and shareholder return program

SK Hynix said it had discontinued its review of a potential U.S. IPO for its flash memory and solid-state drive subsidiary, Solidigm. “The IPO was intended to raise external capital for the expansion of Solidigm’s production facilities,” SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh Jung said. “However, after carefully considering recent financial market conditions and other factors, we concluded that proceeding at this time would not be the best way to achieve the originally anticipated outcome. We have therefore discontinued our review.”

Hwang commented, “The Solidigm IPO raised issues around a dual listing… If the returns aren’t flowing back to shareholders, it’s very difficult to re-rate the stock.” Additionally, SK Hynix unveiled an expanded fiscal year 2026 shareholder return program of 100 trillion won (~$75 billion), including cash dividends over 30 trillion won (~$22 billion) and buybacks exceeding 60 trillion won (~$45 billion), supported by Kioxia investment gains.

Solidigm is currently in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department to invest $45 billion in a new U.S. chip plant, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the negotiations. Before committing to what would be the first new major flash-memory chip production facility on American soil, Solidigm is seeking U.S. government permission to send equipment to upgrade an existing plant in Dalian, China. 

Data center pullback and Samsung catching up

Counterpoint Research warned of risks such as pullbacks in cloud spending. “The single most severe threat would be a scenario reminiscent of 2018, where cloud service providers simultaneously pull back on their order volume,” Hwang said. “We anticipate that Samsung will surpass SK Hynix from the HBM4 generation, leading the market share in 2027.”

SK Hynix management said it expects to preserve its market lead through proprietary packaging and customer partnerships.

data.title: Intel Wants a Quantum Business, Classiq Could Help Build One
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

Intel has spent more than a decade developing the components of a quantum computer, from silicon spin-qubit chips to control electronics and software. Now, with its proposed acquisition of Classiq, the company is looking to turn that research effort into a business.

Classiq develops software that helps users design quantum algorithms and run them across different hardware platforms. For Intel, the company adds a layer at the top of the quantum computing stack, along with relationships with enterprises that are preparing for a time when quantum computers can solve commercially valuable problems.

Intel expects the transaction, which is subject to regulatory approvals, to close in the first half of 2027. The company did not disclose the purchase price.

“We haven’t really done much by way of customer engagement or trying to commercialize our technology,” Intel CTO Pushkar Ranade said on a media call. “We believe we have most of the elements of the quantum computing stack except for the very top platform layer,” which Classiq provides.

The acquisition would allow Intel to offer capabilities extending from quantum chips and control electronics to the software used to develop applications, Ranade said. It would also mark a change in the way Intel views its quantum work.

“This is not going to be a high-margin business from day one,” he said. “This is really a bet on the future.”

That future depends not only on Intel’s ability to scale its own spin-qubit technology, but also on its ability to serve an industry pursuing several competing approaches. Intel said it intends to maintain Classiq’s support for other quantum hardware platforms.

From gates to applications

Classiq was founded on the premise that software would become a bottleneck as quantum hardware advanced, said co-founder and CEO Nir Minerbi.

Early quantum software development was largely limited to gate-level programming, a process he compared to designing a chip at the transistor level. Classiq set out to raise the level of abstraction, allowing developers to describe what they want a quantum program to do while its software synthesizes a circuit.

“We embraced many of the technologies that allowed scaling up in classical computing, like EDA technologies, modeling, synthesis, compilation,” Minerbi said on the media call.

That approach, he said, has allowed enterprises, academic institutions, and governments to begin building quantum teams without requiring every member to be a quantum computing expert. Specialists in a particular industry can contribute knowledge of their own problems while working with people who understand quantum algorithms.

Minerbi said companies using Classiq include BMW, Lufthansa, Comcast, Wells Fargo, and Merck. They are developing applications, building teams, and creating intellectual property as they prepare for more capable quantum hardware.

“All of them are preparing for the day when commercial value could be extracted from this hardware,” he said.

The distinction matters: Customers can use the software to explore and prepare applications today, but Minerbi’s description does not mean those applications are already delivering a commercial advantage on Intel quantum processors.

Intel’s existing software will sit below Classiq’s platform. Classiq synthesizes algorithmic quantum circuits, which then flow into Intel’s hybrid quantum-classical compiler and runtime, according to Anne Matsuura, Intel’s senior director of quantum software and system architecture.

“Our compiler deals with both the quantum and classical parts of a quantum program, and it separates them and optimizes them separately,” Matsuura said on the media call.

Matsuura also clarified that Classiq’s algorithmic circuits are different from the physical circuits and wiring in a quantum computer. Its software operates several layers above the hardware. That division of work reflects a broader challenge in quantum computing: connecting an end user’s problem to hardware whose characteristics vary from one system to another.

Izhar Medalsy, co-founder and CEO of quantum software startup Quantum Elements, sees the two companies as bringing complementary capabilities. In his view, Classiq focuses on translating end-user problems into quantum circuits, while hardware providers must address the characteristics of their particular systems.

“Classiq has done a strong job of understanding enterprise needs,” Medalsy told EE Times. “The acquisition is a signal that Intel wants to engage more directly with end users and their applications.”

Quantum Elements approaches the stack from closer to the hardware, using digital representations of quantum processors to help develop software for different systems. Medalsy described its work and Classiq’s as complementary.

Intel’s spin-qubit bet

Intel has chosen silicon spin qubits as the basis for its own quantum hardware. Unlike some competing approaches, spin qubits can be made using processes related to those used in semiconductor manufacturing—a potential advantage for a company with Intel’s fabrication experience.

Ranade said Intel makes qubit chips and control electronics at its fab in Hillsboro, Oregon. The company calls the respective processes 18AQ, with the Q standing for quantum, and 18AC, with the C standing for cryogenic.

The qubit process uses interconnect geometry and design rules based on Intel’s 18A technology, Ranade said, although the process used to make the qubit device itself is distinct and requires some specialized equipment. He said more than 90% of the process equipment is the same.

Owen Lozman, managing partner of Copenhagen-based quantum investment fund 55 North, sees Intel’s semiconductor manufacturing and packaging capabilities as strengths. The company has also demonstrated an ability to run development and testing cycles quickly, he said. But even with those advantages, Intel faces challenges in scaling spin qubits into a useful quantum computer.

“There are a lot of engineering challenges to overcome, even if you get the physics right,” Lozman told EE Times.

Among them are achieving uniformity across spin qubits and managing the wiring and control signals needed as systems grow. Lozman’s fund has invested in Groove, another company developing spin-qubit technology; he said 55 North does not hold a position in Classiq.

While that hardware development continues, Lozman sees value in giving developers software to prepare applications and understand the resources their algorithms will require. He said the acquisition brings Intel an experienced team working on a layer of software it did not previously own.

“I think you have to kind of move early,” he said. “I think they get an early mover advantage.”

The neutrality question

Intel’s commitment to spin qubits gives it a clear direction for its own hardware. Classiq, however, has built its platform to work across a broader field, where companies are pursuing different approaches and the eventual leaders are not yet clear.

That creates a question for Intel: Can it use Classiq to strengthen its own quantum offering while maintaining the confidence of customers and hardware providers that rely on the software to work across platforms?

For Medalsy, independence matters. His company also works with multiple hardware partners, and he said customers pay close attention to whether a software provider is tied to a particular system. “I think keeping yourself independent and not coupled to any specific hardware provider is extremely important,” he said.

Intel said it intends to continue supporting Classiq’s existing integrations and maintain a hardware-agnostic platform. Medalsy believes the company will have to manage the concerns that come with changing ownership. “Time will tell if the industry will accept that as a neutral play or maybe more of a fully integrated approach,” he said.

Asked what commitments or safeguards would maintain partners’ confidence, Minerbi said the reaction so far had been positive. He argued that hardware vendors need access to end users and that Classiq can help provide it. He did not identify specific safeguards during the call.

Intel’s explanation for keeping the platform open rests on a broader view of its role in the industry. Although its own qubit development will remain focused on spin qubits, Ranade said Intel is open to providing foundry services, photonics, and advanced packaging to companies pursuing other modalities.

“We are completely agnostic to the modality” when it comes to the Classiq platform, he said. “Our intent is to have Classiq continue to support all modalities.”

According to Minerbi, the combination could allow Intel to engage with other hardware providers as well as end users. Those relationships could give Intel customers for its manufacturing capabilities while extending the reach of Classiq’s software.

Lozman said he believes Intel has good reasons to preserve that breadth. Supporting other platforms can give the company visibility across the ecosystem, he said, while helping it recover the value of its investment. But Intel will need to manage those relationships carefully, he said, balancing the advantage of ownership against the value of a platform used by others.

“It’s not easy,” Lozman said. “It will take a lot of discipline.”
